| §50.5: the frustum family answers **84 of 84** | §49.6's 84 was configurations on which a **rule** held, never answers. Pre-wave: 38 answered. Post-wave: **53**, with 0 refused for want of an order where 44 were, and all 31 remaining stopped in `select.rs` |
| §50.2 item 4: naming beyond the coaxial pair is unsafe **because of cone-against-cone** | a **non-coaxial cone and pipe can share a line** — a pipe of radius 2 about `(1,0,1)` through `(0,2,0)` holds the ruling `(t,0,t)` of `Cone::new(Axis::z(), 1.0)`, since `‖(p−o)×d‖² = 8 = 4‖d‖²`. Two families rest on `intersect`'s refusal, not one |
| a lane report: the parabola knife edge is **not reachable with rational numbers** through the public door | `E` is homogeneous of degree 2 in `n`, so normalizing divides it by `L²` and moves no sign, and the division rounds exactly at **power-of-two ratios**. `Cone::new(Axis::z(), 0.5)` against `Plane::from_point_and_normal((0,0,4), (−1,0,0.5))` is a parabola with whole-number points |
| `NO_POINT_MAY_USE_ALL_OF_ITS_BOUND`: the worst a search finds is about **3·ε** against a published 256·ε | true of three planar rows. The quartic control sits at **0.738 of its bound**, about 189·ε; the headline 0.429, the band 0.477 and rising with corpus width |
| the fuzz file: repacking would reinterpret **every one** of the 824 seeds | **92**, or 42 for the narrower repack |
| `plane.rs`, mine: turning a wall round twice is the plane it started as, **bit for bit** | false for a plane storing `-0.0`, which my own fix had just made possible |

Two of the six were written into §50 before any lane ran, and both were the same
error: **quoting a row from an earlier section without opening what it measured.**
§50's preamble says every file and line it cites was checked against the tree by
opening the file. That was true of the file citations and false of the numeric
ones, and the distinction is the whole finding.

### 51.5 §49.7's prediction fired, on one site

> *"The next unit will ship a correct fix that carries a rounded test into a place
> where it decides an answer."*

**Fired, on the presort and only there.** Six of the seven call sites the ordering
predicate reached carry their own derivations and hold up under reading. The
seventh — the hint sort in `nodes_along`, which the building lane's own table
omitted — is a rounded `total_cmp` justified by a sentence inherited verbatim from
the straight-crossing case: *"every neighbouring pair is then proved."* It was
not. `merge_points_that_are_one_point` asked and acted **only on `Decision::Zero`**,
discarding a `Neg`. A gate swapped one pair in the hint and got **8 tests failing
with wrong answers, not refusals**.

Nobody could make the rounded key actually wrong — instrumented, the topo suite
stays green at soak factor 8 with 1024 proptest cases, and the instrument fires
immediately when inverted. So there was no demonstrated defect and no proof
either, and the sentence claimed one.

**The fix is not the assertion the gate proposed**, and the reason belongs in the
record. The hint is a rounded read of the **caller's** coordinates, so asserting
on it puts caller data into a panic; and `order_along` is holding the right answer
at that exact line, which makes it §16.10's **gap** — refusing over an answer
already in hand is the family the rule names. `prove_the_hinted_order` turns the
hint into the order by insertion sort over the proved comparison. The gate's swap
experiment, re-run against the fix, changes nothing: 586 of 586 pass with the hint
deliberately scrambled, for straight crossings and for bends.

### 51.6 The prediction for the next unit

Six sentences, four consecutive units, and the countermeasures already tried are
§15.10's case list (works), the fail-condition brief (works), and the closing gate
(works — it caught five of the six). What none of them reaches is a sentence
written **before** the work, in the planning section, quoting an earlier unit.

> **The next unit's largest error will be inherited from a section it quotes, not
> produced by a lane.** Score it at the next gate by taking every number §51 or
> the next planning section cites from an earlier §, opening what that § actually
> measured, and checking the reading. The countermeasure is cheap and specific:
> **a planning section may not cite a number from an earlier section without
> naming the test or command that produced it.** A row that cannot name one is
> quoted as prose, not as a bound.

**A claim that other claims rest on is stated once, in a fixed phrase, and cited
rather than restated.** The test of whether a load-bearing sentence is written
well enough is whether one grep finds every place that leans on it.

That is the half the rule above was missing, and it has a demonstration rather
than an argument behind it. *Grep for the reason, not the conclusion* is useless
when the reason was paraphrased three different ways and only one of them sat
near the distinctive word. It happened in `rscene`'s design doc, to the sentence
"coarser is likelier to succeed": written three times in three wordings, killed
by this unit's pointed cone, and retired in exactly the one place its editor
happened to be working. The other two survived their own evidence, and were
found by luck.

### 51.8 What was learned about running the work

- **Five lanes at once, then three, three and one.** Write sets were named before
  any lane started and every merge was clean — no conflict in seventeen lanes.
  The cost of that discipline is that a lane which finds a defect one file outside
  its set must hand it back; the benefit is that four of them did, and each
  handback became the next lane's whole deliverable.
- **Briefs that name what counts as *failing* keep working.** Third unit running.
  Every one of §51.4's corrections came from a lane or gate contradicting its own
  brief — which only happens if the brief says what a wrong answer would look like.
- **Two gates, split by numbers and by claims, beat one gate.** Each found things
  the other did not, and each disagreed with a lane. A gate is also not exempt:
  the claims gate published corpus kind counts that did not sum to `743 × 2`, and
  the lane that re-derived them said so and showed the arithmetic.
- **A `sonnet` lane staged its whole deliverable and never committed it.** The
  brief said commit as you go; had it been killed, all of it was lost. Worth a
  hook rather than another sentence in a brief, on §50.8's reasoning that
  recording a rule has been tried.

### 51.9 One pipe, one name — the reversal folded, the slide left open

Run after §51 was written, on the row §51.7 listed second.

**The false sentence is the finding.** `name_of_the_surface_either_way_round` —
the helper written for exactly this problem, which already folded a plane's
facing — ended its doc with *"A ball and a pipe have no reversed form at all and
are their own key."* A ball genuinely has none: its centre and its radius are all
it holds and neither has a sign to turn round. **A pipe has one, and so do a cone
and a bend.** `Axis::reversed` keeps the origin and negates the direction, so
`Cylinder::new(Axis::z(), 2.0)` and `Cylinder::new(Axis::z().reversed(), 2.0)`
are one surface holding different numbers in three of nine slots. A cone is
double-napped and a bend's centre cannot move, so turning either round is the
same point set too. **A §16.10 negative claim, carried as a paragraph, inside the
function whose whole job was this class** — the seventh sentence of §51.4's shape
and the one that had been load-bearing longest.

**Turning a stored axis round moves no corner, and it is measured.** 72 curved
surfaces against 153 plane pairs plus 36 same-bend curved pairs against 18
planes, every subset of the axes turned round: **12 960 comparisons, 7 584 of
them placing corners, 0 differences** — same points, same order, bit for bit,
refusals matching refusals. The instrument is live: swapping the reversal for an
origin *slide* of 0.1 gives **587 of 12 960 differing**.

**It renumbers no `which`, for a structural reason.** `which` counts along the
line the **two planes** cross in; `how_it_sorts_against` compares the kind first
and two of three must be flat to be solved at all, so a curved surface is always
the third row and the line is fixed by the other two. `three_planes_faced_the_one_way`'s
stated reason for handing curved triples over untouched — *"turning a plane round
turns that line round"* — is about a **plane**, and does not carry to an axis.

**The fold went in the geometry key and nowhere else.**
`name_of_the_surface_either_way_round` and `names_of_the_three_surfaces` fold the
axis direction the way they fold a plane's facing. **Not**
`how_it_sorts_against` or `name_of_surface_bits`: their job is a total order on
stored numbers, folding there makes two distinct bit patterns compare *equal*,
and `canonical_cut_surfaces` then dedups on a tie broken by whichever face handed
its cuts in first — reintroducing the order dependence the fixed order exists to
remove. And no curved analogue of `three_planes_faced_the_one_way`, because the
sweep says the solve was already neutral and there is nothing for one to do.

**No fuse-level test passes, and the wall is demonstrated rather than asserted.**
Two spellings of one pipe need two solids carrying that pipe, i.e. coincident
cylindrical faces, and the fuse refuses that first — `Undecidable`, *a point
inside a piece of a face*, enclosure `inf`, identically for one spelling and for
two, found independently by both lanes. So the fuse-level row is a **pin in
§51.1's shape**: it asserts the refusal is the same whichever way the pipe is
written, and fails the day the wall moves.

**A fifth spelling freedom does not exist**, and that is counted rather than
asserted: stored numbers against real degrees of freedom are plane 4/3, ball 4/4,
pipe 7/5, cone 7/6, torus 8/7, and every leftover is the direction's length, its
sign, or the pipe's slide. A negative radius or a negative slope is refused, not
folded; a torus with its radii swapped is a different surface; a cone's apex and
a torus's centre are determined points. **Why the slide is a pipe's alone**: a
plane stores one offset number where a pipe stores a whole three-number origin of
which only the part across the axis matters, so two in-plane points either round
to one offset or make two planes a rounding apart — never two names for one.

### 51.10 The cheap form of a gate: a reader with a reason to be adversarial

§51.8 records that a closing gate which re-derives every load-bearing number
beats one that reads the lane's report. This unit found the cheap form of the
same thing by accident, at the very end, and it is worth having because a gate
costs a lane and this costs a sentence.

**What happened.** A downstream consumer was told, in conversation, that a full
circle is walked in *at least four steps* however coarse the deflection is —
true, and `by_turning`'s quarter-turn cap is why. They restated it as *at least
four points* and said they were about to turn it into a compile-time assertion.
That sentence is wrong: `walk.rs:349` is `let points = (1..steps)`, both ends
excluded because the ends are the corners, so `steps` steps emit `steps − 1`
points and the floor is **three**. It was caught in the minute between their
saying they would pin it and their pinning it.

**A correct number in the wrong unit**, which is §51.4's family with a shorter
fuse: *at least four* was true of steps and silent about points, and the two
differ by exactly the ends-excluded rule both sides had already written down.

**The active ingredient is not the test.** Nobody re-read the sentence more
carefully. What happened is that the claim acquired **a reader with a reason to
be adversarial about it** — being about to be pinned made it worth opening the
emit line rather than trusting the recollection. A test is a reliable way to
manufacture that reader on a schedule; the announcement of one manufactures it
for free. So, alongside §51.6's rule:

> **Telling the owner of a fact that you are about to depend on it is most of a
> gate at none of the cost.** The moment to do it is when the claim is about to
> become load-bearing, because that is when being wrong is expensive and
> therefore when somebody will actually look.

**And pin the mechanism, not the arithmetic.** The fix was not to pin `>= 3`.
A pinned point count moves for two different reasons — the cap changing, or the
emit arithmetic changing — and a reader hitting the failure cannot tell which.
Pinned as *a closed run is cut into at least four segments*, a failure means the
quarter-turn cap or the fewest-steps floor moved, which is a sentence somebody
can act on. Correct and useless is a real category.

**One argument for not copying a fact across a boundary**, better than the usual
one. The usual reason is that two copies can disagree. The stronger reason is
that a copy restated in the copier's own words can be **wrong and internally
consistent**, and then it passes — where two copies that disagree are the case
you find out about. Facts rcad measures are asserted in rcad's suite and cited,
never restated, by anything downstream.

## 52. Four rows closed, two of them by being wrong, recorded 2026-09-05

*Six lanes and two gates against §51.7's four defect rows. `just default` green
twice at the end, 1698 tests. Written from the gates' verdicts rather than the
lane reports; where a gate and a lane disagreed, the one that re-derived from the
tree wins. Every number below names the command or test that produced it, which
is §51.6's own rule applied to a record and not only to a plan.*

### 52.1 Two of the four rows were wrong about themselves

| row | what it said | what it was |
|---|---|---|
| `room_left_over` records nothing | a defect, plus *a caller cannot tell* | defect real, **second clause false** |
| an empty walk on a closed edge | unknown behaviour | **not a defect** — refused twice over |
| the pointed cone refuses coarse | a refinement-geometry accident | **a §16.10 gap in the bound**, fixed |
| an oblique plane cutting a cylinder | a gap, past 60° of tilt | **false, and backwards** |

That is the finding to carry forward. §51.7 was written by a unit that had just
audited itself carefully, and half its defect rows still misdescribed the defect
they named — not by being vague, but by being specific and wrong. Every one of
the four was **stated with a mechanism**, and the two that were wrong were wrong
about the mechanism while being right that something was there, or right that
nothing was there for the wrong reason.

### 52.2 Row 1 — a wave-through now leaves a record

`room_left_over` (`walk.rs`) hands a tolerant caller an empty point list when the
crossing's own rounding eats the whole deflection. Two of its three sibling sites
carry a signal and it carried none. It now takes a `log: &mut ProvenanceLog` and
pushes one record on that path.

**The threading never leaves the file**, which is what made this the small lane it
looked like: `walk` already had a log, and `walk_an_endless_bend` — which did not
— is called only from `walk`, twice.

The record follows the precedent already in the crate, `DynamicRange::check_under_policy`
(`scale.rs:243-261`), which records a check that is not a predicate the same way:

```rust
Record::new(ROOM_LEFT_TO_REFINE_A_WALK, &[], Level::Float,
            Decision::Undecidable { enclosure: deviation }, Measures::Length)
```

`Measures::Length` makes `record.wobble(ws) == deviation` for every working size —
`dimension = 1` makes the fold at `policy.rs:241` the identity — so this record
cannot turn an accepted walk into a refused solid: the same number just passed
`policy.wobble_is_acceptable` at the push site.

**The stronger form of that, which a gate established and the lane did not:** a
fuse never sees one of these at all. `fuse/mod.rs:183` is the only line outside
tests that compares a log's `worst_wobble` against a budget, and instrumenting it
to record any `room left to refine a walk` it met produced no file across all 1698
tests. `walk` is reachable only from `mesh.rs` and from `validate.rs`'s
`the_ring_a_wire_traces`.

`crates/rcad-geom/tests/a_waved_through_walk_leaves_a_record.rs` fails 2 of 4 on
`22a163a` and passes 4 of 4 here. Its other two are anti-vacuity halves and they
are load-bearing: moving the `log.push` to fire unconditionally fails both.

### 52.3 The clause that was false, and why its replacement needs three exits

§51.7 said the empty list *"a caller cannot tell from a stretch that legitimately
needed no interior points"*. **It could.** `FEWEST_STEPS_THAT_SHOW_A_BEND`
(`walk.rs:930`) is 2 and both step counts floor at it, so neither emitting range
can come out empty; the only other empty-points exit carries a deviation of
exactly `0.0`; and on a wave-through the deviation is at least the deflection,
which `Deflection::of` refuses to let be zero. So
`points().is_empty() && deviation().magnitude() > 0.0` already *was* the
wave-through, and the fix is the log record alone.

**That argument has three exits from `walk` and not two**, and the third is the
one a reader will miss. `follow_the_quartic` (`walk.rs:666`) returns a positive
deviation and never calls `room_left_over`, so it never pushes a record. The
claim survives only because `march` cannot come back empty: on its first
iteration `travelled = 0.0`, so the early return is false and a point is pushed
before any exit can be taken. A gate ran this as a live invariant over the whole
suite — asserting the equivalence on every `Ok` return — and it never fired.

### 52.4 Row 2 — refused twice over, and the answer is scoped

An empty walk list on a **closed** edge never reaches a consumer, because
`SolidView::mesh` refuses the whole mesh and `points_along_edge` is never
published for that solid at that deflection.

**Two independent barriers, demonstrated rather than read.** A closed edge is the
only edge of its cap's wire, so that loop has one corner and `Loop::through`
refuses it — `TooFewCorners { count: 1 }`. The wall's wire is *not* one corner, so
that check says nothing about it, and it is refused separately by
`AWireWillNotLieFlatOnItsFace`. Independence was shown by loosening
`Loop::through` (`domain.rs:27`) from `< 3` to `< 1`, watching the cap through,
and catching the wall underneath — done once by the lane and again from scratch
by a gate.

The shape it takes is the finding. The deflection floor and the crossing's own
rounding are deliberately in step for an ordinary bar, so a closed edge cannot be
starved on one. They come apart when a **cap plane leans hard**: a bar of radius
1 with its top cap normal `(2e9, 0, 1)`, at `Policy::tolerant(1e11)` and
deflection `5e-4`, has two closed edges that answer differently — the flat bottom
circle walks into points, the leaning top's ellipse comes back with none.

**Scope, and it matters downstream.** What is demonstrated is *no route the suite
can build*, not *never*. A face whose wire held the closed edge **alongside other
coedges** all meeting at that vertex would contribute one corner instead of *n*
and could still clear the three-corner rule — and then a `Mesh` holding an empty
list for a closed edge would exist. Nobody reached the question of whether a
builder or the deserialize door can make such a wire. §52.11 keeps it.

### 52.5 Row 3 — the bound charged a ruling

The pointed cone refused at 1e-3 of its own size with finer deflections meshing
either side. Reproduced exactly on `22a163a`: **6 of 21 deflections refused, 9
finer ones meshed anyway, the ladder changes its mind 6 times**
(`cargo nextest run -p rcad-topo --test whether_a_coarser_deflection_always_meshes
the_pointed_cones_refusals --no-capture`). §51.7's numbers were inherited
correctly, which is worth saying because most of this section is about ones that
were not.

**A §16.10 gap, and the answer was one step from the end of a derivation already
written down.** `how_far_a_flat_piece_of_a_cone_strays` goes
`Σλᵢrᵢ(1 − cos(uᵢ − u_k)) ≤ maxᵢ rᵢ(1 − cos Δ)` and then bounds every corner's
radius by the patch's largest, collapsing it into one chord. **A corner at the
apex has `rᵢ = 0`**, and a triangle with two corners on the apex is a *ruling* —
in 3D it is the segment from the apex to its third corner, lying exactly on the
cone and straying nothing. The old bound charged it `0.7071·v`. The fix keeps
each corner's own radius.

The refusal was `RanOutOfRoomBeforeMeetingTheDeflection` from `refine_the_inside`,
with the packing floor `step/8` declining both wanted midpoints. It is not the
`√d`-against-`d` crossing the fixing lane wrote down — see §52.8.

**What actually moved** (1e-4 of size, the 140-line family sweep diffed between
the two trees): the five cone and frustum solids, `53742→32812`, `56880→14550`,
`31666→29144`, `71648→724`, `77874→1026`. The other fifteen solids are
line-for-line identical at every rung.

The pointed cone now meshes every rung from `0.2` (44 triangles) to `1e-5` (6488)
and is stopped instead by how many points a patch will hold —
`MoreTrianglesThanAPatchWillHold` from about `5.96e-6` down, `would_need`
6 282 880 at 1e-6. That limit is **monotone**, and provably so:
`a_step_that_stays_within` builds its step from `radius` and `share`, neither of
which depends on the deflection, and `refuse_a_patch_too_big_to_hold` runs before
a single point is placed. Once it says no it says no all the way down.

### 52.6 Row 4 is backwards

§51.7 expected `BoundarySideStraysFurtherThanTheDeflection` past roughly 60° of
tilt where a plane cuts a cylinder. **It never fires**, at any tilt, on either of
two probes built through the public API — a bar cut by a leaning plane, and the
shape the row itself names, a bar fused against a turned cube, swept to 89.5°.

The measurement inverts the row. At `r = 0.05`, deflection `5e-4`, tilt 89.4°, the
wall's 570 boundary sides split into 502 on the tilted ellipse at `0.005222` of
the deflection and 52 on the **flat bottom circle** at `0.486075` — the tilt
making a side **cheaper by 93×**. The worst consumer of the boundary budget on
that solid, at every tilt, is a plain un-tilted circle.

**The expected one-line fix was already in the tree**, and this was settled by a
prediction rather than by reading. `how_many_steps` was hand-computed for both
candidate reaches: `Δu = 1.251631e-2` for the ellipse's own `r/cos θ` against
`1.208305e-1` for the cylinder's `r`. Observed: `1.25163e-2` on the ellipse's
sides and `1.2083e-1` on the bottom circle's, where the reach genuinely *is* `r`.
Both candidates visible in one run, every digit matching. `Conic::how_far_it_reaches`
is `across.length().max(and.length())` and `where_a_plane_cuts_a_pipe` stores the
semi-major in `and`, so the walk has always stepped against the ellipse's reach.

**The negative claim, earned properly on the second attempt.** The first attempt
argued that a smaller reach could not cross the threshold, which is backwards — a
smaller reach gives a finer step and a *smaller* stray. The real argument is the
budget split: `WHAT_A_BOUNDARY_SIDE_IS_REFINED_TO` is `3/16` of the deflection
(`mesh.rs:2117`) and the constant's own doc derives that the triangulator reads at
most `8/3` of what the walk was asked for, so `strays ≤ (8/3)(3/16)·deflection =
deflection/2` for **any conic, any reach, any tilt**. Demonstrated over 747
configurations and 159 110 boundary sides: nothing fired, worst `0.498389` on a
cylinder and `0.49347` on a sphere — 99.7% of the ceiling, which is what makes it
a demonstration and not a paragraph. Scoped to the solids `build.rs` builds and
fuses of them; a cone or a torus is untested and `Model::builder().add_face` is
public.

### 52.7 A test that could not see the bound it measured

**The unit's largest finding, and no row named it.** `triangulate.rs` carries a
§15.6 search for how much of the cone's published bound a real triangle uses. It
reported `0.39447768211554846` after the fix against `0.39447768211554857`
before — **one ulp, after a change that cut a frustum's mesh from 56 880
triangles to 14 550.**

Not luck. The search's family was `[[0, far], [span, far], [span/2, near]]` — two
corners on the same widest ring — and for that family the collapsed bound and the
per-corner bound are *algebraically identical*, both `2·t·far·sin²(span/2)`. All
240 triangles evaluated the same number under both formulas. The search was
measuring a bound the code no longer computed, and the doc comment above it still
stated the old claim word for word.

The replacement family is 12 rows × 8 slopes × 6 spans = **576 triangles**, and it
carries its own proof that it can tell the two apart —
`what_the_collapsed_bound_would_have_charged` runs beside the real bound on every
one:

| shape | new ÷ collapsed |
|---|---|
| the six old `[far, far, near]` rows | exactly **1.0** — the blindness itself |
| frustum bands 1→2, 1→3, 2→8 | 0.5, 0.3333, 0.25 — that is `near/far` |
| a corner on the apex | 0.125 – 0.197 |
| the 48 rulings | **0** — bound is slop, collapsed charges the whole span |

Worst share on the new family is `0.6589159410563914`. Putting the collapsed
radius back fails the search rather than moving its number.

**The general shape:** a published bound was tightened and its own §15.6 search
could not see the tightening, because the search's family sat exactly on the
subspace where the two formulas agree. A test can be blind to the thing it exists
to watch, and green is what that looks like.

### 52.8 Eight false sentences, and where each sat

§51.4's shape for the fifth consecutive unit. The new column is *who could have
caught it*, because that is what changed this time.

| the sentence | what was true | caught by |
|---|---|---|
| §51.7: a caller cannot tell an empty walk from a stretch needing no points | it could; §52.3 | the lane, checking its own brief |
| §51.7: the ellipse's `r/cos θ` outruns the deflection past 60° | backwards — the tilt makes a side cheaper by `cos θ` | a spike told to distrust the row |
| §51.7: refining against the ellipse's own reach is a one-line change | already in the tree since `Conic::how_far_it_reaches` was written | the same spike |
| a lane: **no mesh anywhere got coarser** | meshes of cones got much coarser — 3.9× on a frustum with no apex, which was not the bug. The claim that survives is that the bound is still an *upper* bound | a gate diffing the family sweep |
| a lane: the ragged edge is the packing floor's `√d` crossing the height's `d` | that predicts a monotone floor; the data is a **band**. The strays ladder is `1.4142/2^k`, the same at `d = 2e-4` and `2.518e-4` | a gate instrumenting the loop |
| a lane: B's leaning cap is *the same one-line change in what `walk` is handed* | three quantities, not two; §52.9 | two gates, from opposite sides |
| a spike: neither probe refuses | one refuses in 8 of 20 cells, in the **fuse**, over the whole 30–70° band the row blamed. The conclusion survives because the other probe covers that band; the sentence does not | a gate re-running the probes |
| a spike: eight boundary sides it could not explain | **sixteen**, and they are `cut_in_two` cuts rather than walk steps — the mismatch between two independently walked chains, bounded by their half-sum `6.67e-2` against `6.3544e-2` observed | a gate told to go and find out |

Seven of the eight sit **beside a number that was right**. That is now four units
running, and the countermeasure that worked here is not a better sentence — it is
that somebody re-ran the thing the sentence was about.

### 52.9 §51.6's prediction, scored: fired, on a surface it did not name

> *The next unit's largest error will be inherited from a section it quotes, not
> produced by a lane.*

**Fired, and the scoring is not close.** The two rows that were wrong about
themselves were both inherited from §51.7 verbatim, and one lane inherited
§51.7's proposed fix into its own handback without checking it. The counter-example
is that two of the eight false sentences were lane-produced.

**But the largest error was not a number at all, and that is the new part.** The
blind search in §52.7 is an inherited *test*: the doc comment stated a claim from
before the fix, and the fixing lane changed the code under it without opening what
its test measured. §51.6's countermeasure — *name the test or the command that
produced a number* — would not have caught it, because the number was produced by
exactly the test that was named, and the test was wrong. So:

> **When a fix changes what a published bound computes, the bound's own §15.6
> search must be shown to move.** A search whose number does not change is not
> reassurance; it is the first thing to distrust. Show it failing under the old
> formula, the way a test is shown failing without its fix.

**And the cheap gate of §51.10 paid again, twice.** A peer session independently
derived the row-4 correction and sent it over; it arrived after the spike had
already demonstrated it, which turned an agreement into a confirmation. The other
direction paid too — telling that session which run confirmed its facts, rather
than that it was right.

### 52.10 The leaning cap, and a §19 nerve

Sized by a gate rather than named, because the row it came from was about
something else. The mesher's deflection floor
(`how_far_a_mesh_point_of_this_face_rounds`, `mesh.rs`) is built from a face's
**corners** plus the surface's radius. For a leaning cap that under-charges, and
the measurement is stark: the floor is **flat at `6.1432e-13` at every tilt**,
while the walk's own demand is `256·ε·(lean + 0.5)`. The walk crosses the floor at
a lean of about **10.8**, and by `lean = 2e9` the floor is claiming nine orders of
magnitude of deflection workable that are not — off by `1.85e8×`.

**The runaway term is not the one anybody named.** It is not the ellipse's
semi-major. `Conic::size` is `how_big_this_is([middle, axis.origin()], …)` where
`middle` is the ellipse's **centre**, so it grows with *where the conic sits* up
the pipe's axis. Measured `closest` matches `256ε·(lean + 0.5)` and not
`256ε·√(lean² + 1)`.

That is a §19 nerve, and the code says so itself.
`Conic::how_far_it_reaches`'s doc comment reads *"Where a circle sits is not
allowed to change how finely it is cut (§19)"* — and today where it sits does
change how far off it the kernel says its points are. A **gap**: the answer
exists, and the floor cannot see it.

### 52.11 What stands

| open | where |
|---|---|
| **the leaning cap under-charges the deflection floor** | §52.10. A §19 nerve with a number: crosses at lean ≈ 10.8, `1.85e8×` at `2e9`, and the term is the conic's stored `size` rather than its reach |
| **the wave-through record says `Undecidable` for an event that chose to go ahead** | nothing was undecided; a policy accepted a wobble. `Cause::TolerantFallback` is the honest cause and `Record::resolve_to` is `pub(crate)` to `rcad-predicates`, so `rcad-geom` cannot write it. A **gap in the API**, not a design choice, and it has two consumers already — this site and `scale.rs:243-261`. The constructor asked for is `Record::an_operation_settled(operation, inputs, approximation, measures)`, which adds no `Cause` variant and so pays none of §25.8's renumbering cost |
| **a wire holding a closed edge alongside other coedges** | §52.4's unreached route, and the one way an empty list could still reach a `Mesh`. Nobody established whether a builder or the deserialize door can make one |
| **the `crowded`-only route to `RanOutOfRoomBeforeMeetingTheDeflection`** | reached by nothing. Tallied over the workspace: that refusal came back **once in 1694 tests**, with `crowded = 0, declined = 2`. Recorded on the variant's own doc |
| ~~**`Mesh::triangles()` publishes two claims and guards one**~~ | **closed.** `mesh.rs:61-70` promises *faces in the solid's stored order* **and** run-to-run stability; only the second bit, because the nearest test collected `triangle.face()` into a **`HashSet`** (`meshing_a_curved_solid.rs:728-735`) which passes under any permutation, and `measure.rs:662` needs only that the order is *fixed*, not that it is the stored one — so a stable but different order kept every sum bit for bit and broke the promise silently. Both halves hold, and are now pinned as **two separately-named tests** in `what_order_the_mesher_hands_its_triangles_back_in.rs`, each shown failing under its own mutation: permuting whole face-blocks breaks stored order and leaves contiguity intact, which is what proves the two are independent. Raised by a consumer announcing it was about to depend on it — §51.10's third payment, again catching rcad's own gap |
| **a test that walks the same iterator as the thing it tests** | not a defect, an averted one, and worth the row because it is §52.13's shape one level up. `Mesh` emits in `SolidView::faces()` order and "the solid's stored order" *is* `SolidView::faces()` — so a test comparing the two would have moved with the mesher and stayed green while the promise broke. The pinning tests therefore read arrival order off the **geometry** instead: a bar's blocks must be a plane facing `[0,0,-1]`, a plane facing `[0,0,1]`, then a face that is no plane at all; a cube's must be its six exact outward normals. Exact `f64`, no tolerance. **A test must not derive its expectation from the machinery under test**, and the cheap check is whether the expected value would change if the code did |
| **two shells sharing one face slot is refused, and the test names a narrower case** | `validate.rs:427-433` counts face uses with `for shell in shells.values()`, so the count is **global across shells** and `Invalid::UsedMoreThanOnce { entity: "face" }` catches a slot two shells both list. The only test, `a_shell_that_lists_the_same_face_twice_is_caught` (`validate.rs:2418`), exercises **one** shell listing a face twice. The invariant is wider than the test that names it, and the wider half is the half a consumer met — a face arriving twice with two placements, which downstream is a wrong picture drawn confidently. The guarantee also holds only for a model that has been through `validate()`, which the deserialize door does but a hand-built `Model` need not |
| **why the pointed cone's old ladder was ragged rather than one floor or one band** | each individual refusal is settled; the *pattern* was never worked out, and the file now says so rather than carrying the `√d`-against-`d` sentence that did not fit the data |
| **the frustum tightening's own demonstration** | §52.7's new family covers it now, but only at the patch level. No solid-level test exercises a frustum band the way `a_cone_patch_that_reaches_its_apex.rs` covers a pointed cone |
| **`three_surfaces.rs` wants two flat surfaces** | unchanged. Still the wall for `AFrustumAgainstABar`, 96 of 96 |
| **one pipe, two names, from an origin slid along its own line** | unchanged; §51.7 |
| **`fuse(A, B)` and `fuse(B, A)` refuse with different provenance** | unchanged; §51.7 |
| **`cuts.rs` and most of `three_surfaces.rs`** | unchanged, still unaudited; §51.7's warning about the grep stands |
| **the fuzz decoder draws 3 of 5 kinds** | unchanged; §51.3 |
| **the rest of §51.7** | unchanged |

### 52.12 What was learned about running the work

- **Both gates found the one regression and no lane did.** `a_solid_with_a_cone_face.rs`
  pinned a refusal that the cone fix legitimately removed, and the lane that made
  the fix never ran the workspace suite. Two gates, split by lane rather than by
  numbers-versus-claims, each found it independently on their first full run.
  §51.8's *two gates beat one* holds for a second unit, with a different split.
- **A spike with an empty write set costs nothing to run concurrently.** Row 4's
  file was unknown, which normally serialises it behind whichever lane might own
  it. Made read-only, it ran beside all three lanes and returned the answer that
  the row needed no lane at all.
- **Correcting a brief's own premise before dispatch worked twice.** The row-4
  spike was told its row's expected fix looked already-present, and told to check
  that rather than believe it. It checked, and came back with the prediction that
  settled it. The same brief shape gave the row-1 lane §51.7's false clause as
  *something to establish before fixing*, and it established it was wrong.
- **A lane that would not substitute one confident sentence for another.** Told
  that its `√d`-against-`d` mechanism was contradicted, the lane declined to write
  the gate's replacement mechanism either, because it could not establish that one
  without instrumenting dead code. It wrote that the pattern was never worked out.
  That is the right answer and it should be easier to give than it is.
- **Handbacks stayed cheap because write sets were named first.** Six lanes, seven
  merges, zero conflicts. Four handbacks, and three became another lane's whole
  deliverable.

### 52.13 The prediction for the next unit

§51.6's prediction fired and its countermeasure was shown to have a hole — a
number can be produced by exactly the test that was named, and the test can be
blind. So the next one is about tests rather than sentences:

> **The next unit will find a test that passes for a reason other than the one it
> was written for.** Score it by taking every test whose failure would be the sole
> evidence for a published bound, and mutating the thing it claims to watch — not
> the code near it. A test that stays green under that mutation has been found.

The countermeasure is cheap and it is already written down in two places this
unit: a test earns its keep only if somebody has seen it fail for its own reason.
`a_waved_through_walk_leaves_a_record.rs`'s anti-vacuity halves were mutation-checked
and survived; the cone bound's §15.6 search was not, for years, and did not.

**The three specimens have a sharper shape in common than "a weak test".** Not one
of them is a weak assertion. Each is a *strong* assertion about something smaller
than the doc above it promises:

- a `HashSet` of faces, standing for an order (§52.11);
- a triangle family sitting exactly where two formulas agree, standing for a
  bound (§52.7);
- `a_shell_that_lists_the_same_face_twice_is_caught`, standing for a counter that
  runs over every shell (§52.11).

So the thing to look for is not a test that asserts too little. It is a **test
whose name describes a narrower case than the invariant it stands for**, which is
findable by reading names against docs and needs no mutation to spot.

### 52.14 A wrong unreachability claim is worse than none

The rule in CLAUDE.md already says a claim that something cannot be reached needs
a demonstration and not a paragraph. This unit adds the part about **which way the
error points**, and it earns its own section because the two directions have
opposite costs.

`docs/decisions.md` §16.10's rule is symmetric in the claim and not in the
consequence. A wrong claim that something *can* happen leaves dead code and wastes
a reader's time. **A wrong claim that something cannot happen invites the deletion
of live code, and hands the reader the argument for deleting it.** The comment is
not merely wrong; it is an accomplice.

This unit's own specimen is the spike's negative claim in §52.6 — *only a reach
below `r` could cross the threshold* — which was argued rather than demonstrated,
was backwards, and would have justified not writing the sweep that later measured
159 110 boundary sides. The claim it replaced is a demonstration, and the
difference is not rigour but direction: the second one can be run.

> **An unreachability claim cites where the refusal actually happens** — the
> file and the line that does the refusing — and not where the writer assumes it
> does. Same discipline as citing a test rather than restating it, and for the
> same reason: a cited refusal can be opened and checked, a remembered one cannot.

A consumer hit the same shape twice in one week from opposite directions, and
reported it; that it was found independently outside this repo is why it is
recorded as a shape rather than as one more row.

**A partial justification is the dangerous case, not an absent one.** Applied as
a sweep at the consumer's end the same afternoon, the rule caught a false claim
on its first pass, and the way it had survived is the part worth keeping: the
claim covered **two of four** cases and gave a good reason for those two, so it
read as *more* thorough than a claim covering none — and therefore deterred the
checking that an obviously bare assertion would have invited. A missing reason
advertises itself. A reason that is sound about half its subject does not, and it
is the half nobody looks at that is load-bearing.

So when a negative claim covers several cases, the number it covers is part of
the claim: *none of these four is reachable* wants four citations or an argument
that visibly ranges over all four, and anything less is written as covering what
it actually covers.

**And the way an unchecked fact gets in is that nobody thinks it is a claim.**
The restated measurement in `docs/consumers.md` that §52.11's handedness row
sends a lane to replace did not arrive as a demand or a specification. It arrived
as a courtesy — one side telling the other something it had noticed, offered
rather than filed — and an offered observation does not feel like it needs a
citation to the person offering it, nor like it needs checking to the person
merging it. It becomes a claim the moment it lands in the other side's file, and
by then both of the people who could have doubted it have already decided it was
not that kind of sentence.

> **A fact about rcad written down in rcad's tree is a claim, whatever the tone
> it arrived in.** The test is where it ends up, not how it was offered.

## 53. A plane, a cone and a coaxial pipe — the unit after four rows closed, recorded 2026-09-05

*Planning section. Written before any lane runs, against `main` at `97525a9`.*

**Every number below was re-derived from the tree and names the command that
produced it.** That is §51.6's rule, and §52.9 showed it has a hole — a number
can come from exactly the test that was named, and the test can be blind — so
§53.7 charge 3 covers the hole and §53.9 extends the rule to a spike.

### 53.1 The name, and what the unit is

`three_surfaces.rs` wants two flat surfaces. That row has been open for two units
— §51.7 opened it, §52.11 carried it unchanged — and it is the wall
`AFrustumAgainstABar` stops at, having been let through `intersect` by §50's work
only to stop one step further down.

Re-derived on this HEAD by

```text
cargo nextest run -p rcad-topo --test how_often_a_fuse_with_a_cone_refuses \
    how_often_a_certified_fuse_with_a_cone_in_it_refuses --no-capture
```

> `a frustum against a bar: 96 fuses, 0 answered, 96 refused (100.0%):`
> `{"geometry: where three surfaces meet is only worked out when two of them are`
> `flat, and fewer than two of these are": 96}`

So the family is not merely at zero: **every one of its 96 refusals is this one
wall, by name**, which is what makes it a consumer for §13's purposes rather than
a wish.

**This unit is not the general one-flat solve.** `error.rs:571-576` classes that
as a **gap** and not a limit — the points are there and a real algebraic solver
reaches them — whose family of fixes is Dupont–Lazard–Lazard–Petitjean machinery
or a certified numerical solver with a separation bound of its own, and both are
a milestone rather than a lane (§31.2).

This is the narrow reduction that avoids it: **two curved surfaces crossing in a
conic put that conic in a plane, so `{P, S1, S2}` becomes `{P, Q, S1}`, which the
existing two-flat road already solves.**

**It is a third road of a shape the file already has, not a new mechanism.**
`error.rs:566-569` names the two that run today — two pipes the same way with a
cap plane, which is a union of two overlapping parallel bars; and a ball and a bar
both resting on a block's floor — and `meet_of_three_surfaces`'s own doc refuses
only *"when neither road back to two of them runs"*. A cone and a coaxial pipe is
the third. That matters for where A puts it and for how much of `three_surfaces.rs`
it is entitled to disturb: **the answer is a road beside `where_a_plane_and_two_quadrics_of_one_bend_meet`
(`three_surfaces.rs:591`), not a new solver.**

### 53.2 Six corrections, before any lane reads them

They exist because §51.6's countermeasure keeps being walked through, and one of
them is §52.14's shape found in the wild before a lane ran.

1. **`arrange.rs:1232` does not panic, and the line is 1232.** An earlier reading
   in planning said 1233 and said it could panic. `u8::try_from(which)` fails only
   above 255 and `which` reaches 3. The `expect("three surfaces meet at most
   twice")` **message** is false; the code is safe. A false message is D's
   deliverable, not a bug.

2. **`MeetOfThree::At` already promises four points, and it lives in the spine
   lane's own file.** `three_surfaces.rs:88`. Its doc already reads *"one, two,
   three or four"* — a straight line meets a ring four times, which is what makes
   a torus not a quadric. **What the reduction breaks is not the count. It is the
   order clause**, *"running along the line the two planes cross in"*, which
   cannot survive two **parallel** planes because there is no single line. Planning
   had this as an `arrange.rs` job beside the spine; it is inside the spine's file
   and cannot be concurrent with it.

3. **§51.3's "76 bytes" is right for two of the three pairs it names and wrong for
   the third**, and the conclusion it supports is untouched. `BYTES_PER_NUMBER = 5`
   (`crates/rcad-geom/tests/fuzzing/mod.rs:59`) and one kinds byte, against
   `Cone { axis, slope }` = 7 numbers and `Torus { axis, ring_radius, tube_radius }`
   = 8:

   | pair | bytes |
   |---|---|
   | a torus against a cone | `1 + 40 + 35` = **76** |
   | a torus against a pipe | `1 + 40 + 35` = **76** |
   | a torus against another torus | `1 + 40 + 40` = **81** |

   The sentence at `every_pair_of_surfaces_the_fuzzer_draws_is_named_honestly.rs:56`
   says 76 for all three. **This is §52.14's specimen exactly**: a reason sound
   about two thirds of its subject, which therefore reads as more thorough than a
   bare assertion and deters the checking a bare one would invite. The conclusion
   survives in all three cases, because the longest seed checked in is 71 —
   re-derived by `find fuzz/corpus/where_two_surfaces_cross -type f -printf '%s\n'
   | sort -n | uniq -c`: **824 seeds, longest 71, 280 of them exactly 71, shortest
   1**. 71 is also `MOST_BYTES_A_PAIR_READS` (`fuzzing/mod.rs:64`), so the corpus
   number and the decoder's cap agree because the fuzzer was told the cap — it is
   not independent evidence, and §53 does not use it as any.

4. **Parabolas and hyperbola branches are moot for the reduction.** They are
   produced only inside `where_a_plane_cuts_a_cone`, so a *curved* pair never
   crosses in one.

5. **No `walk.rs` type needs to be made public.** The identity touches neither
   `Conic` nor the normalized `up`.

6. **`cuts.rs` and `three_surfaces.rs` are in different crates.**
   `crates/rcad-geom/src/three_surfaces.rs` is 2110 lines;
   `crates/rcad-topo/src/fuse/cuts.rs` is 495. §51.7 and §52.11 name them in one
   breath as *the unaudited pair*, which reads as one lane's worth of one crate's
   work and is two crates. §53.4 splits the audit on that line.

### 53.3 The sentence the unit earns

> **Where three surfaces meet is worked out when a cone and a pipe are proved
> coaxial and one plane cuts them.**

Falsifiable two ways, both measured rather than argued:

- `where_one_plane_and_two_curved_surfaces_meet` (`three_surfaces.rs:543`) has a
  road for the coaxial cone-and-pipe pair, placed **after**
  `what_a_plane_that_grazes_one_of_them_leaves` (`three_surfaces.rs:934`) so that
  no answer that road gives today moves; and
- `MeetOfThree::At`'s order clause is replaced by one that survives two parallel
  planes.

**The sentence does not promise 96 of 96 answered, and neither does any lane.**
The reduction's domain is the triple `{plane, cone, pipe}`. A triple of the 96
holding no plane at all, or two curved surfaces that are not a coaxial cone and
pipe, is outside it and stays refused. What is promised is that **the wall moves
and the pin is re-derived to whatever the measurement then is** — which is what
the pin's own text already demands: *"re-derive the number over this whole family
and pin the measured one — do not relax it to a floor and do not guess it
(§19.1)"*. Promising the 96 here would be a number invented before its
measurement, which is the thing four consecutive units have been caught doing.

### 53.4 The shape of the waves, and what each lane may write

| step | one deliverable | may write |
|---|---|---|
| **A the spine** | the reduction: `the_two_flat_surfaces_in_a_fixed_order`, the new road, and `MeetOfThree::At`'s replaced order clause | `crates/rcad-geom/src/three_surfaces.rs`, `crates/rcad-geom/tests/where_a_plane_a_cone_and_a_coaxial_pipe_meet.rs` (new), `crates/rcad-geom/tests/where_a_coaxial_cone_and_pipe_cross.rs` |
| **B the geom audit** | every site in `three_surfaces.rs` where a bare `f64` decides something, reported | **nothing. Read-only** |
| **C the fuse audit** | the same over `crates/rcad-topo/src/fuse/` — `cuts.rs`, `bake.rs`, `arrange.rs` | **nothing. Read-only** |
| **D the contract** | `arrange.rs:1232`'s false `expect` message | `crates/rcad-topo/src/fuse/arrange.rs` |
| **E the pin** | `AFrustumAgainstABar` re-derived, not relaxed | `crates/rcad-topo/tests/how_often_a_fuse_with_a_cone_refuses.rs` |
| **G1 the numbers gate** | charges 1 and 3 | its report |
| **G2 the claims gate** | charge 2 | its report |

**A, B and C run concurrently.** B and C have **empty write sets**, which is
§52.12's own finding put to use — *a lane with an empty write set costs nothing to
run concurrently* — and it is what makes wave one three lanes rather than two,
which is what CLAUDE.md's floor of three would otherwise have caught here.

**Splitting the audit by crate is not bookkeeping.** §51.8 and §52.12 both record
that two gates beat one *and that the split matters*, each finding what the other
did not. The same argument applies to an audit, and here the split is free: the
two files are in two crates, `cuts.rs`'s neighbours are `bake.rs` and `arrange.rs`
rather than anything in `rcad-geom`, and a lane that has to hold two crates' worth
of call graph in its head is the lane that runs past forty-five minutes. **C reads
`arrange.rs` and D writes it**, which is not a conflict because D is wave two, but
it is named here so that nobody makes them concurrent later.

**D and E are wave two, behind A.** Neither can be written before A has settled
what the order actually is: D's message and E's number both describe A's result.
D is one string and is not a lane on its own — it is dispatched with whichever
audit handback lands beside it.

**Wave two's real size is not known now, and that is deliberate.** B and C's
handbacks become wave-two lanes, named at dispatch. §51.8 and §52.12 both record
that a handback became the next lane's whole deliverable — four times and three
times respectively — so reserving the room is a plan and guessing the contents is
not.

### 53.5 The rules whose pass and fail are written before the lane runs

Fourth unit running (§47.6, §49.5, §51.8, §52.12).

- **A fails** if it makes any `walk.rs` type public; if it changes any answer
  `what_a_plane_that_grazes_one_of_them_leaves` (`three_surfaces.rs:934`) gives
  today; if `MeetOfThree::At`'s replacement order clause is anything weaker than
  *a fixed order depending only on which three surfaces they are* — the doc is in
  A's own file, so leaving the old sentence standing is a fail and not an
  oversight; if it states the domain wider than **a cone and a pipe proved
  coaxial**; or if the new road introduces **any division, or any comparison on a
  bare `f64`**.

  That last one is the spine's own claim turned into its fail condition. The whole
  reduction rests on the pencil identity being exact — products and sums of stored
  numbers, with `t` never computed — so a division appearing on the road means the
  claim in §53.9 is false. It is also mechanically checkable, and it is exactly
  the class §51.2's volume sign and §51.7's audit row are about: **A must not
  quietly become the thing B and C are looking for.**

- **B and C fail** if either writes anything under `crates/`; if a reported site
  is given without its file and line; or if a negative claim — and an audit's
  output is mostly *"this one is fine"* — is stated without citing **where the
  refusal actually happens**, per §52.14. A paragraph is not a demonstration.

  **The threshold, and it governs whether §53 keeps its spine.** The count is
  **wrong answers only, not missing arguments.** A site with no written argument
  means *write the argument, or write the test* — the spine survives. A site that
  gives a **wrong answer** becomes the next lane's whole deliverable. **Two wrong
  answers and §53 changes spine**, because at two the unaudited pair is the unit
  and the reduction is not.

- **D fails** if the replacement message states a bound the code does not enforce.
  The current one is false in exactly that way, and replacing one false message
  with another is worse than leaving it, per §52.14's direction-of-error rule.

- **E fails** if it relaxes the pin to a floor, or pins a guessed number, or
  reports the family's rate without re-deriving it over the whole family.

**At forty-five minutes a lane commits what is done, writes what is left, and
hands back** (CLAUDE.md). A's handback point is named: the exact-planes helper and
its tests land as one commit, the road that calls it as a second, so *what is
left* is never a tree that does not compile.

### 53.6 What stays out

| out | why |
|---|---|
| **the general one-flat solve** | a milestone by `error.rs`'s own doc. §53.1 |
| **three curved surfaces** | no plane, no reduction, and no consumer asking |
| **the fuzz decoder widening** | §51.3, corrected by §53.2 item 3. Wants the corpus re-minimised with it, which is a lane of its own |
| **`ResultIsNotManifold` with `count` other than 1** | unchanged since §51.7 |
| **`Conic::size` grows with where the conic sits** | §52.10's runaway term. Recorded as a row with its numbers — crosses the floor at a lean of about 10.8, `1.85e8×` at `2e9` — and **offered to whoever takes `walk.rs` next**. It is a §19 nerve and it is not this spine |
| **§52.11's `Record::an_operation_settled`** | out, **with a written condition**: if B, C or any wave-two lane lands in `rcad-predicates` for its own reasons, this is that lane's second deliverable. It adds no `Cause` variant and so pays none of §25.8's renumbering cost |

**§51.7's other rows are not restated here.** The writer, fillets, the torus,
cone against cone, the slid pipe origin, the split provenance — all unchanged, all
already written down once. §51.10 argues that a copy restated in the copier's own
words can be wrong and internally consistent, and then it passes; §53 cites
§51.7 and §52.11 rather than reproducing them.

### 53.7 The gates' three charges, split across two gates

1. **Numbers.** Re-derive every load-bearing number from the tree, independently
   of the lane that reported it — including the ones in this section.
2. **Claims.** `claim-audit` over every negative claim in the two audited files,
   and over B's and C's own reports. Not instead of a code review.
3. **Mutate what each load-bearing test claims to watch, and confirm it fails.**
   Take every test whose failure would be the sole evidence for a published bound,
   and mutate the thing it claims to watch — not the code near it.

**Charge 3 is how §53 scores §52.13's prediction**, and it exists because §52
walked straight through §51.6's *name the command* rule and the rule did not help.
The cone bound's §15.6 search reported `0.39447768211554846` after a fix, against
`...857` before — one ulp, under a change that cut a frustum's mesh from 56 880
triangles to 14 550. The triangle family sat exactly on the subspace where the old
and new formulas agree. **The number came from precisely the test that was named,
and the test was blind.** A search whose number does not change under a fix that
changes what it computes is not reassurance; it is the first thing to distrust.

Charges 1 and 3 go to G1, charge 2 to G2. Split by kind rather than by lane, which
is §51.8's split; §52.12 used a per-lane split and found the same regression twice,
so both splits work and neither is the point — **two gates is the point.**

### 53.8 The machinery this unit was going to change, and does not

**Nothing. §53 dispatches against the tree as it stands.** §50.8 changed six
things before its spike ran and each earned its place. This unit's one candidate
did not, and why it did not is worth more than the guard would have been.

**A guard against a lane staged-but-uncommitted.** §51.8 asked for it after a
`sonnet` lane staged its whole deliverable and never committed it, and reasoned
*"had it been killed, all of it was lost"*.

**The shape it was asked for cannot be built, and finding that out cost one
question.** Planning settled on *a blocking `SubagentStop` hook*. Against the
published hooks reference:

- **`SubagentStop` cannot block.** It runs **after** the subagent has already
  completed, so exit code 2 has nothing left to stop. It is a post-action hook and
  it runs for side effects only.
- **It fires** on normal completion, on failure, and on a user-initiated stop.
- **Whether it fires on a forced kill is not documented either way.** The
  documented *"does not fire on user interrupts"* is about `Stop`, the
  session-level event, and does not carry to `SubagentStop`.

**Two mechanism claims were made in planning this unit and neither survived
opening the reference**, which is why this reads as a finding and not as a
paragraph of setup:

| the claim | what is actually established |
|---|---|
| §51.8: the hook would have saved work *"had it been killed"* | it cannot block and it runs after the lane is done, so it saves nothing on any exit; and the kill case is undocumented rather than covered |
| §53's own first draft: *"`SubagentStop` does not fire when a subagent is killed"* | **not established.** The docs are silent. The sentence was inherited from `Stop`'s documented behaviour and restated about a different event |

The second one is this section's own, and it is the shape §53.10 predicts —
**a claim carried by nothing, written into the section that argues against claims
carried by nothing.** It was caught because the sentence was about to become
load-bearing and therefore acquired a reader with a reason to be adversarial
(§51.10), which is the third time that has paid and the first time it has paid
against rcad's *planning* rather than against its code. **A correct fact about
`Stop` restated about `SubagentStop`** is §51.10's *at least four steps* restated
as *at least four points*, one repository over.

**What the guard is for, restated on what is left.** Not loss prevention — no
hook event reaches a killed process. **Handback honesty**: a lane must not report
*done* with its deliverable staged and uncommitted, so the merge step cannot miss
it.

**And it is not built.** Three shapes remain buildable — a report-only
`SubagentStop` hook, one that commits the staged work itself, or a `just` recipe
at the **merge gate**, which is the only one a test can drive — and none of them
is bought. §51.8 wanted a hook because *recording a rule had been tried*; that
argument was made about the heredoc ban, where thirteen lanes produced three
offenders. **The staged-and-never-committed failure has happened once, cost
nothing, and the guard now available is weaker than the one that was asked for.**

That is §13's rule pointed at machinery rather than at a feature: a part with no
named consumer is not built, and *one lane, once, no loss* is not a consumer.
The row stays open and this section is where the next unit finds the mechanism
already worked out, so the question does not have to be re-derived to be
re-decided.

**Both false claims here were found by opening a reference nobody had opened**,
at a cost of one question. The lesson is not about hooks: **the machinery section
is where a unit is likeliest to spend effort on something whose justification
nobody checked**, because machinery is the part that gets no test and no gate
charge. §53.7's three charges cover lanes and tests; nothing in this record has
ever scored a claim about the harness.

### 53.9 The spike passed, and every claim it makes names the test that will carry it

Branch `worktree-agent-a48dec4c50ee6f0fc`, commit `f743ea4`, 442 lines added to
`three_surfaces.rs` in a `#[cfg(test)] mod spike_two_circles_are_two_planes`.
**Probe code is never merged.**

The identity, which is the whole spine: for the pipe's stored direction `w`, its
stored radius `r`, and the cone's apex and slope `s`,

> `t²·Q_cone − Q_pipe = (r − s(x·w))(r + s(x·w))`

so the two flat surfaces are `s·(w·p) = s·(w·apex) ± r`. **A pencil identity, not
the `r/slope` scaling route.** Every number in it is a product or a sum of stored
ones; nothing divides, and `t` is never computed.
`what_a_stored_plane_and_an_exact_one_share` (`three_surfaces.rs:816`) admits the
two planes **unchanged**.

**Q16's rule, applied to §53 itself.** A spike's code is deleted and its
conclusions are not, so each conclusion below names the merged test that will
carry it. A row with no test is written as prose and is not leaned on.

| what the spike established | the merged test that carries it |
|---|---|
| the two planes are exact and need no division | `the_reduction_finds_all_four_corners_with_no_width_and_no_log` — asserts an **empty** provenance log, so a certified answer that logged anything fails it |
| the merge yields **four** points, not two | the same test |
| the order is invariant under the pipe's stored direction | `the_pipes_stored_direction_flips_the_order_the_corners_come_out_in`, whose spike form demonstrates the flip **and** the fix; the merged form asserts the invariance |
| the order is invariant under the cone's stored direction | `the_cones_stored_direction_moves_the_order_as_well` |
| no answer the grazing road gives today moves | `the_grazing_road_and_the_reduction_agree_where_both_answer` |
| the scaling worry does not exist — `Axis::new` scales the direction to length one before storing, so two pipes down one line hold the same three numbers up to sign | `a_pipe_built_from_a_longer_direction_stores_the_scaled_one`. **Not in the planning handoff's list of the spike's findings**, and it is the one that closes off a whole family of spellings |
| the triple is refused today though all four corners are whole numbers | `today_the_triple_is_refused_though_all_four_corners_are_whole_numbers` — the failing-first test CLAUDE.md rule 2 asks for |
| a turned axis, where nothing lands on a whole number, is answered | `a_turned_axis_is_answered_by_the_reduction_and_refused_by_the_road` |
| **the domain is one pair of surface kinds — a cone and a pipe proved coaxial, not a family** | **no test carries this.** It is a scope statement and it is written as prose, which is why it is A's fail condition (§53.5) rather than an assertion |

**Ordering was a no as built, and the fix is demonstrated rather than argued.**
The same bore stored as `[0,0,1]` and as `[0,0,-1]` gave the same corners in two
orders. Pinning the shared normal's sign by its first exactly-nonzero component,
and sorting the two offsets by an exact `minus().sign()`, makes them identical.
That canonicalization is the load-bearing part of A's first commit, and §53.7
charge 3 re-runs it rather than reading about it.

**What the audit's site count is, and is not.** A recon pass in planning reported
**14** sites where a bare-`f64` result feeds a comparison, sign test, division or
`Decision` — 10 in `three_surfaces.rs`, 4 in `cuts.rs` — against **4** hits for
the comparison-operator grep §51.7 already warns is not evidence. **Neither number
is quoted here as a bound.** A naive `[<>]=?` sweep on this HEAD returns 159 lines
in `three_surfaces.rs` and 23 in `cuts.rs`, most of them generic brackets, so the
4, the 14 and the 159 are three different questions and none of them has its
criterion written down. **B's and C's first deliverable is a count with its
criterion stated**, and §51.7's instruction stands unchanged: follow every
`f64`-returning call, and — §52's addition, found twice behind a **bound** rather
than a comparison — every place a sum is collapsed to a max.

### 53.10 The prediction for the next unit

§51.6 predicted an inherited claim and fired. §52.13 predicted a blind test and is
scored by §53.7 charge 3. Neither reaches the thing §53 is actually built on.

**Two consecutive units have now been planned around a spike whose code is never
merged**, and §52.8 already carries two false spike sentences — *"neither probe
refuses"*, when one refused in 8 of 20 cells; *"eight boundary sides"*, when there
were sixteen and they were not what the spike called them. A spike's evidence is
deleted at the moment its conclusions become load-bearing.

> **The next unit's largest error will be in a claim its spike made that no merged
> test carries.** Score it by taking every sentence in the planning section
> sourced to the spike and naming the merged test that would fail if it were
> false. A sentence with no such test is the specimen.

The countermeasure is cheap, specific, and already applied to this section:
**a planning section citing a spike names the merged test that will carry the
claim, or writes the claim as prose.** §53.9 is that table, and its last row —
the domain statement, carried by nothing — is the section declaring its own
specimen in advance rather than waiting to be caught with it.

That row is also why the earlier candidate for this prediction was withdrawn.
*"The audit's worst site will be in neither audited file"* is nearly checkable in
advance from §53.4's own brief, which already orders B and C to follow every
`f64`-returning call across file boundaries. A prediction its own plan half
guarantees is not one.

## 55. Nobody owned a worktree, recorded 2026-09-06

§54 is left for §53's unit record. This section is numbered 55 because a peer
session had already claimed 54 for that, in a handoff rather than in this file —
which is, in miniature, the whole subject of this section.

### 55.1 The alarm, and what was actually wrong

Sessions kept reporting *"another session is live in my worktree"*. Five Claude
sessions really were in this repository on the evening of 2026-09-05, so most of
those reports were true. One was not: a dispatcher had sent a second agent into a
worktree its own first agent still held, and could not tell the difference.

It could not tell because **nothing recorded who owned a worktree.** Not the
harness, not git, not the skills. Every method available was the wrong shape:

- `ps aux | grep claude` is worse than nothing. It matched twenty processes across
  three unrelated repositories, several stopped since June — and it cannot see the
  hazard at all, because **a subagent runs inside its parent's process**. The two
  agents that actually collided were one pid with one working directory.
- `ListAgents` lists peer sessions but shows no working directory, and sessions
  rename themselves mid-flight; one message bounced for that the same evening.
- A handoff document is a memory, and `/clear` had already destroyed what it was
  remembering. The 2026-09-05 handoff said *"No lanes running"* on the writing
  agent's own initiative. Nothing had checked, and nothing could have.

### 55.2 The demonstration

Measured 2026-09-05 and 2026-09-06 from the session transcripts under
`~/.claude/projects/-home-mattias-git-mattiasgronlund-rcad/` and from a probe.

| Fact | How it was shown |
|---|---|
| Two agents shared one worktree for 27 minutes | `agent-a0f7fc3c66d82650c` ran 18:25:48Z–19:54:40Z in `rcad-worktrees/spike-floor`; `agent-accf6823fe09975e8` was dispatched into the same worktree at 19:27:22Z |
| A report is not the end of a lane | the dispatcher had sent that spike three questions by `SendMessage`; it answered the first at 19:26Z and the dispatcher dispatched over it 100 s later |
| The harness does not lock what it creates | a live `isolation: "worktree"` agent reported **no `locked` line for its own worktree**, and no worktree in the repository was locked while it ran |
| The harness *does* set the agent's working directory | that probe's own `pwd` was its worktree |
| A hand-made worktree does not | every subagent in the 2026-09-05 transcripts has `cwd` = the primary tree, including those whose brief named a worktree |
| No worktree carried an owner | no `.git/worktrees/*/locked` file existed at 22:45Z, `spike-floor` included, with a live agent in it |

### 55.3 What it cost, on one evening

- A spike lost both its remaining answers: its probe was SIGTERMed mid-run and its
  output file filled with the other agent's output.
- A `just default` "green twice" that the dispatcher itself flagged as measured
  over another writer's uncommitted work, in a merge tree shared with a live
  session.
- A clean fast-forward merge handed back to the user undone, because `main` was
  checked out in the worktree that session was writing.
- An accidental write to the primary tree, from a lane that had to `cd` to reach
  the worktree its brief named — *"the second time today"*.
- `just prune-worktrees` crashing on a locked worktree, fixed the day before.

### 55.4 The lock is the record

**A worktree's git lock is this repository's statement of who owns it.** It was
chosen over inventing a registry for one reason: it is the only candidate that
survives the session that wrote it. It is a file in `.git/worktrees/<name>/locked`,
not session state, so `/clear` cannot lose it and a session that never dispatched
the lane can still read it. `prune-worktrees` already honoured it. Locking blocks
only `worktree remove` and `worktree prune`, so it never obstructs a lane.

**The reason string is ASCII.** `git worktree list --porcelain` C-quotes a reason
holding any non-ASCII byte — a `·` reaches a porcelain reader as `\302\267`. This
was found by `check-lanes-selftest` on its first run, which is the argument for
having written it. `just lanes` sidesteps it by reading the lock file directly;
`prune-worktrees` matches on the listing and does not.

### 55.5 What changed

| # | change | what proves it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `just lanes` — every worktree, whether held, by whom, and whether dirty | `just check-lanes-selftest`, in `default`; builds a repository with a held and a free worktree and asserts the reason comes back verbatim |
| 2 | `.claude/hooks/worktree-create.sh` locks what it creates, naming the agent and the ISO time | `.claude/hooks/check-worktree-create.sh`, in `check-hooks`; fails with *"came back with no lock"* when the lock is stripped out |
| 3 | the shared-tree memory drops `ps aux` for `just lanes`, `ListAgents` and `git status` in the specific tree | not in this repository; it is a user memory |
| 4 | `delegating`: `just lanes` before dispatching into an existing worktree, and **a lane is finished when its worktree unlocks, not when it reports** | prose |
| 5 | `handoff`: a required "still in flight" section, generated from `just lanes` and `ListAgents` rather than recalled | prose |
| 6 | `delegating`: the merge tree is yours alone and is not where anyone else has `main` checked out; unlock as you merge | prose |

Items 4–6 are prose because they are judgements about when to dispatch, not
behaviours a command can check. Items 1 and 2 are the ones that had to be
mechanical, and both carry a test that fails without the change.

### 55.6 What this does not close

**Nothing releases a lock automatically.** The create hook writes one; the
dispatcher is told to unlock at merge; if it does not, `prune-worktrees` keeps the
worktree for ever rather than reclaiming it. That is the safe direction to fail —
§50.8's 166 GB came from the other one — but it means an abandoned lock is rubbish
only a person clears, and the ISO date in the reason is the only thing separating
a live lane from a dead one. A `SubagentStop` hook that unlocks is the obvious
next move and is deliberately not built here: §13 wants the consumer named first,
and one run's worth of locks is not yet that consumer.

### 55.7 A claim this section does not make

The investigation was first written up around the sentence **"a subagent outlives
the session that dispatched it"**, and it is not in this section because it was
never demonstrated. Its one specimen was an agent still writing after its parent
session's apparent death, with a `/clear` fifteen seconds later that looked like
the successor. The parent was idle between turns, not dead: it went on to send a
long message twenty minutes afterwards. The `/clear` had started a different
session in a different terminal, which has six events and never ran.

Two timestamps close together were read as cause and effect and nothing checked.
Every item above stands on the other rows of §55.2, none of which depend on it.
The claim is cheap to settle — dispatch a long `isolation: "worktree"` agent,
`/clear`, and watch whether its transcript keeps growing — and it is left open
rather than assumed, in either direction.

## 56. A cone's apex after a turn and a shift, recorded 2026-09-06

Three things a consumer raised in a channel overnight, none of which was in any
rcad file when this session started. That is §55's defect, and the answer to it
is this section rather than another reply.

One was a defect that gave a consumer a confidently wrong answer, found by asking
and fixed here. One was a number nobody had measured, and measuring it says the
prediction was wrong by a factor of two — in rcad's favour, and for a reason worth
writing down. The third was fixed by the import lane in `8358620` while this was
being written; §56.6 says what that cost and what caught it.

### 56.1 The demand: exact equality against `Cone::apex()`

rscene shades a cone by asking the surface for a normal, and **a cone has no
normal at its apex.** So its apex triangle is special-cased on *exact* equality
against `Cone::apex()`, deliberately and not for want of a tolerance. A tolerance
there is worse than nothing: a mesh point a whisker off the apex sits on a
genuine ruling whose normal is a genuine answer, so widening the test hands the
wedge middle back for a point that had a right answer available. What the exact
test buys is that a miss is *visible* — the special case does not fire, and the
consumer can say so.

**A miss was therefore a wrong normal and not a refusal**, which is the failure
mode this kernel exists to avoid. rscene could not test it end to end: no
cone-faced solid can be built at their pin. So the equality was rcad's to
demonstrate or to deny, and nothing had checked it.

### 56.2 It was wrong, and only for a face that is both turned and shifted

The two numbers arrive by different routes, and the routes were not the same
movement.

- **The apex a consumer reads** is `FaceView::surface`, placement composed in:
  `Cone::transformed` carries the axis origin through `Isometry::apply_to_point`,
  once.
- **The apex the mesh emits** is worked out where the face is stored — §17.1's
  frame — because `the_surface_this_face_is_meshed_on` reads a placed face's
  surface out of the arena rather than moving it into the meshing frame and back.
  `Cone::point_at(u, 0)` there is the stored apex exactly: both terms it adds are
  zero vectors. That point was then carried out on
  `the_frame_this_face_is_meshed_in(face).inverse()` — and a placed face is meshed
  in its placement's own inverse, so the movement it rode was **the placement
  inverted twice**.

`Isometry::inverse` is not a bit-for-bit involution. It conjugates the
quaternion, which only flips signs, but it replaces the shift with `−R⁻¹t`, which
turns a vector and rounds; inverting again turns it back and rounds again. A pure
shift survives that — the turn is the identity and Rodrigues' form adds nothing —
and so does a pure turn about an axis through the origin, whose shift is zero and
stays zero. **A turn with a shift on it has nothing protecting it**, and that is
the ordinary case: it is what `Model::place_solid` is for and what an assembly is
made of.

### 56.3 The demonstration, and it is a census rather than one example

`a_placed_cones_apex_and_the_point_the_mesh_puts_there`, four tests over 105
placements of a pointed cone of slope a half and height eight.

| family | placements | the doubled inversion moves the apex on | apex missed, before the fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| no placement at all | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| a shift alone | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| a turn about an axis through the origin | 20 | 0 | 0 |
| a turn and then a shift | 80 | 50 | 50 |

The two right-hand columns are the same 50 placements. That correspondence is
what makes this a diagnosis rather than an observation: the misses are exactly
the placements the doubled inversion moves, and no others.

The third column is also what stops the suite passing for the wrong reason. Each
family measures what inverting its own placements twice *would* have cost, and
asserts the count against the sentences above — no pure shift, no pure turn, a
real share of the turns with shifts. Without it the file could go green over a
family that never exercised the bug and look identical.

Worst miss found: one ulp, `[3, 5, 7]` read as `[2.9999999999999996, 5, 7]`.

### 56.4 The fix

`back_out_of_the_frame_this_face_is_meshed_in` rides a placed point out on the
placement **itself**, which is the meshing frame's exact inverse, and falls back
to inverting the frame for an unplaced face — where the frame is
`a_shift_that_loses_nothing`, a negation, and exact either way. Five call sites in
`mesh.rs` took it.

It also makes an existing charge honest. `how_far_placing_this_face_rounds` bills
one `Isometry::POINT_ROUNDOFF` for carrying a mesh point out to where the solid
sits — one movement — and it is now one movement.

### 56.5 The floor at a distance is `18 · ε · L`, measured, and not `36 · ε · L`

rscene's rungs bracketed the floor of a radius-five ball at `1e14` only to
`(0.1732051, 1.7320508]`, and a prediction of **0.79936** had been written down
against it. Nothing had measured it, and `Error::DeflectionBelowWhatAMeshCanReach`
hands `closest` to callers — a published number with nothing checking it (§15.6).

Measured by `the_floor_under_a_placed_ball_is_one_placements_worth_of_rounding_and_not_two`,
at `1f7b75c`:

| the ball is out at | the floor | one placement's worth | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1e6` | `4.239223932641019e-9` | `3.996822872665007e-9` | 1.0606484 |
| `1e10` | `3.996827130754963e-5` | `3.996802890648965e-5` | 1.0000061 |
| `1e12` | `0.003996803131071608` | `0.0039968028886705476` | 1.000000061 |
| `1e14` | **`0.3996802891074774`** | `0.39968028886507634` | 1.0000000006 |

**So the floor at `1e14` is 0.39968, half the prediction.** It sits inside
rscene's bracket, which is why their ladder could not tell the two apart.

The remainder over one placement's worth is `2.4240105997601184e-10` at *every*
distance — the walk's own share, charged against how far the ball reaches in the
frame it is meshed in, and a placed ball is meshed in its own placement's inverse
so it sees a radius-five ball at the origin wherever the solid sits. A
distance-independent remainder is what pins the placement coefficient at one
