rather than merely bounding it under two.

Said without leaning on the test having written the reach down right: the floor
**rises `3.9968028886505635e-15` per unit the ball is placed out, which is one
`Isometry::POINT_ROUNDOFF` to the last bit.** Taken as a slope off the two ends,
everything that does not move with the placement cancels, so that is the placement
term's coefficient on its own.

**Two changes would move these numbers and from outside the crate they are the
same shape.** A second placement term is one. The other is
`how_far_the_points_of_reach` no longer coming to `corners + radius` for a ball's
face — the §15.6 reach under-charge is a live change of exactly that kind — which
would leave the mesher right and this test's arithmetic stale. Both scale the
placement term by a constant, and no measurement of floors separates them. The
assertions say so and name where to look, because the first reading is the
alarming one and would otherwise be the only one offered.

**The number the refusal carries changed while this was being measured, and the
measurement did not move.** The deflection-floor unit landed in `8358620` between
the first run and this one: `room_a_mesh_has_to_work_in` now lets a caller's own
deflection through against `how_far_a_mesh_point_of_this_face_rounds` and
*reports* `the_finest_deflection_the_walk_will_take`, which adds what a step at
the walk's cap stands off its chord. That grew the remainder above by about eighty
— the first run read `3.031649005909485e-12` — and moved no ratio in the table,
because both numbers carry the same `how_far_moving_this_face_rounds` and the
placement term lives there. A test written against a recorded floor would have
gone red for a change that does not touch what it claims. This one is a closed
form and did not.

**Where 0.79936 came from, and it is not a defect in any doc comment.** It was
read out of `the_surface_this_face_is_meshed_on`, whose doc derives `36 · ε · L`
for a surface's movement round trip. That paragraph is the cost of a round trip
the mesher **does not make** — it is the argument for reading a placed face's
surface out of the arena — and it is demonstrated where it stands, by
`a_turned_curved_face_is_not_charged_for_a_round_trip_it_does_not_make`. Taking it
for a term in the floor is the misreading, not the sentence. The floor's terms are
the walk's and `how_far_placing_this_face_rounds`, and for an unplaced face
stored far out, `how_far_shifting_this_face_rounds` at
`SURFACE_AFTER_SHIFTING_ROUNDOFF = 8 · ε` — the 1.44 factor
`a_boolean_that_cuts_nothing_off_a_bar_does_not_make_it_much_coarser_to_mesh`
already measures.

A tolerant caller at `1e14` is cut at `ROOM_ABOVE_THE_FLOOR` times the floor,
which *is* 0.79936 as the floor stood at `c9ff754`. The number was right about the
wrong quantity.

### 56.6 The import census and colour — closed by another lane, and closed wider

The third channel item was `Import`'s doc saying **"what is walked past is counted
rather than forgotten"** in the same paragraph that lists styling among what is
walked past, with only the next clause narrowing the counting to shape-carrying
entities. `SHAPES_THIS_READER_DOES_NOT_TAKE` holds seven keywords and no styling,
so a `STYLED_ITEM` is read past and nothing on `Import` said so. A consumer read
the first sentence, took the census for a complete one, and was about to publish a
denominator saying the importer had dropped nothing out of 367 files — while it
had dropped every colour in all of them. §52.14's shape: a list sound about most
of its subject reading as complete.

**It is fixed in `8358620`, by the import lane and not here.** This session had
written the same fix independently and dropped it on finding the lane's, which is
wider in the part that matters: it also names what happens to a file that carries
styling and *no* solid. That file never reaches the map at all — `Import::read`
returns `TheFileHoldsNoSolid`, or `TheFileHasNoSize` ahead of it — so a caller
using the map as "what did the importer drop" gets an `Err` and never the empty
map it would have branched on. `styling_is_never_among_the_shapes_walked_past`
pins both halves over the real corpus, including the one NIST file with 272
`STYLED_ITEM`s and no solid.

Recorded here because the finding and the fix were two different sessions, and
§55 is about acknowledgements that live nowhere: the duplicate cost one test and
one doc edit, both thrown away, and finding the overlap took one `git diff`.

### 56.7 What this does not close

**Per-face colour out of STEP import is undecided, not refused.** rscene's §8.2
demand is well-formed — `STYLED_ITEM` / `COLOUR_RGB` /
`PRESENTATION_STYLE_ASSIGNMENT` / `SURFACE_STYLE_*` parsed, and a colour per
`FaceKey` on `Import` — and it was acknowledged twice in channel and written into
no rcad file until this line. It is recorded here as outstanding and nothing
more. rscene is **not blocked**: it took the refused path, draws flat and reports
colour unavailable, and its sink is built and tested, so adopting later is
source-side only.

**§56.5 measures a *placed* solid.** A solid whose stored numbers are far from the
origin — what a fuse bakes and what an importer writes — pays
`how_far_shifting_this_face_rounds` as well, and that case is pinned by the 1.44
measurement named above rather than here.

**The apex census sweeps placements, not cones.** One cone shape, 105 placements.
A cone whose stored apex is not at the origin would exercise
`a_shift_that_loses_nothing` on the unplaced path as well, and nothing here makes
one — but that is the **helper's** limit and not the kernel's. The suite goes
through `a_pointed_cone(model, slope, base_height)`, whose signature pins the apex
at the origin. `SolidBuilder::add_face` is public, is re-exported from `rcad`, and
takes an arbitrary `Surface`, so a caller puts the apex wherever it likes in one
line; `rcad-step`'s `cone_from` builds one from any file's placement. Unexercised,
then, and not unreachable.

**But the sweep that would exercise it cannot fail, and that is worth more than
the sweep.** `a_shift_that_loses_nothing` builds its run from the face's corners
*and* `placed_by`, which for a cone is `cone.apex()` itself. Each coordinate is
then either shifted by `low` — where Sterbenz makes `apex − low` exact, and adding
`low` back lands on a representable `apex` — or not shifted at all. There is no
third branch, so the apex comes back bit-for-bit for **any** stored apex, however
far out and however wide the spread. rscene measured one instance of that through
its own facade and got bit-equality; it had measured an identity.

So a census over stored apexes would be a green run over a theorem: an absence
that could not have been a presence proves nothing, which is the same reason
§42.12's tenth criterion makes the import rate carry a control. Written at all, it
needs the doubled inversion of §56.1 as its positive control, the way the 105
placements are the control on the placed side. **What deserves a test is one layer
down** — that the point the mesh emits
is a member of the run the shift is computed over. That is the invariant doing the
work, and it does not transfer: for a sphere `placed_by` is `ball.centre()`, which
the mesh never emits at all. Whether a ball's pole is exact for some other reason
is unmeasured and unasked.

**Nobody ships against any of this today, and the blocker is not the cone.** No
corpus file yields a cone face: 41 name `CONICAL_SURFACE` and none import, and a
census reading `FaceView::surface()` over the 98 files that do import finds 32 094
planes, 945 cylinders, one sphere and no cone. The 41 die upstream of the cone
across 24 unrelated reasons, overwhelmingly `B_SPLINE_CURVE_WITH_KNOTS` on an
edge; `CONICAL_SURFACE` itself maps fine. That day arrives when the B-spline edge
blocker clears, not on any cone work.

**Those four numbers are dated and nothing holds them.** They were taken at
`30d735b` by a throwaway probe walking `RCAD_STEP_CORPUS`, importing under
`Policy::certified()` and censusing `face.surface()` over `import.model().faces()`
— spelling-independent, with the `CONICAL_SURFACE` count a byte scan of the file
so it does not depend on the reader. The probe was deleted, and **no standing test
holds any of it**, so nothing goes red on the day they stop being true. That day
is a named event rather than a vague one: it is the day the B-spline edge blocker
clears, which is the same sentence two paragraphs up. Whether this should be a
standing test instead is §13's question and not settled here — the argument for it
is not the census but the tripwire, and the argument against is that it would be a
test whose subject is another milestone's blocker.

**How this paragraph came to be wrong is the part worth keeping.** It first said
"the public builder this suite goes through does not make one", which is a false
claim about the public builder dressed as a true one about a test helper, and two
readers took it for unreachability and planned around it. The correction then
overreached the other way — that an off-origin apex is "the normal case for
anything imported" — which was an unmeasured consequence asserted inside a
paragraph whose subject was a claim never checked against the public API. The same
shape twice in one thread, in both directions, caught both times by a consumer
reading it back rather than by anything in this tree. §51.10 is the control that
worked; the rule it enforces is CLAUDE.md's, that "no caller hits this" is checked
against the public API and not against today's callers.

## 57. Two ways not to make a 17 000-line file cheaper, recorded 2026-09-06

Two candidates were put up for the cost of reading `docs/decisions.md`: point
rust-analyzer at the tree, or split the file. Both were measured and both are
declined, and the first was declined for a reason worth writing down — it was
aimed at the wrong file.

### 57.1 Where the reading actually goes

Over the 64 transcripts in this project's history, `Read` delivered 2.59 M
characters. By file type:

    .md                64.8%   1.68 M
    .rs                32.8%   0.85 M
    everything else     2.4%   0.06 M

`decisions.md` alone is **0.76 M — 29% of every character `Read` has ever
delivered here**, more than all Rust source in every session combined.
`roadmap.md` is another 0.32 M. Bash delivered 3.90 M over the same span, half
again more than `Read`, so file reading is not even the largest channel.

### 57.2 The 17 000-line file is Markdown

rust-analyzer helps with `decisions.md` by exactly zero, because it does not
read Markdown. The two questions never met: the file that prompted the question
is not a file the tool can open. That is the whole of the answer to the first
candidate, and everything in §57.3 is about the other third.

### 57.3 What rust-analyzer costs and buys on the Rust third

It was driven over stdio against this workspace rather than guessed at:

    cachePriming done                        16.3s
    workspace/symbol usable                  16.4s after a cold launch
    hover on a fn signature                  325 chars
    rust-analyzer RSS                        2.02 GB

Sixteen seconds is not the objection. The objection is the shape of the answers.
`documentSymbol` on `arrange.rs`, the largest file in the tree, needs no index at
all — it is a parse — and returns **78.3 kchars of JSON** for 275 symbols. The
same outline by grep is **2 972 chars** for the 53 top-level items, so for the
query most often wanted the protocol costs 26× the tokens, and a formatter to
fix that is work done to arrive back where grep already was.

What is left is the part text search genuinely cannot do: the type of an
expression, and a definition chased through re-exports. That is real, and it is
narrow, and it would need a JSON-RPC driver plus either a 16-second cold start
per query or a resident 2 GB process beside three other live sessions. It is
deferred under §13 until a named consumer appears; the facade re-export work is
the first plausible one.

### 57.4 The split, and why the recipes already beat it

`decisions.md` is 1.105 Mchars, 54 sections, 452 subsections, median section
17.2 kchars. The case for splitting is that a section is large. It is not:

    just decisions-toc   4 354 chars   all 54 sections
    just decision 41     4 853 chars   §41's prose and its subsection list
    just decision 41.6   3 519 chars
    just decision 8        252 chars

§41 is 79.5 kchars and costs 4.9 to open, because `just decision N` hands back
the section's own prose and then the *list* of its subsections rather than their
text. A file per section cannot beat that, because a file per section still
delivers the section. The effect is already in the transcripts:

    2026-08-30   16 calls   242.0 kchars    15.1 kchars/call
    2026-09-05   16 calls   121.2 kchars     7.6 kchars/call
    2026-09-06    8 calls    16.4 kchars     2.1 kchars/call

The honest argument *for* a split is conflicts — 98 commits touch this file, ten
to thirty a day, at up to +6 900 lines in one day, from as many as four
concurrent sessions all appending at the tail. That pressure is real enough that
§55 opens by explaining a reserved number. But a split only half-answers it: it
removes the textual conflict at the tail and leaves the number collision exactly
where it was. This section is itself the proof: it was written as §56 and had to
be renumbered, because another lane had taken 56 while it was being written.

### 57.5 What was built instead

One gap survived the measurement. Grep answers in line numbers, and a line
number is the one address this file does not take — CLAUDE.md says never to
guess a line range — so every hit cost a walk back up to the heading above it,
and nothing automated that walk. `just decisions-find` closes it by answering in
section numbers, which is what `just decision` wants next.

Its two refusals are deliberate. **The match is case-insensitive**, because of
886 grep commands measured across one day, 97 matched nothing at all, and a
search that misses `Refusal` for a typed `refusal` fails in exactly that silent
way. **No match, and the empty pattern, fail rather than printing nothing**, for
the reason `decision` fails on a number that does not exist: an empty answer
reads as "the decisions say nothing about this", and that is a claim a typo can
forge.

### 57.6 A claim this section does not make

Nothing here says the Rust third is cheap. It is 0.85 Mchars, 33% of everything
`Read` has delivered, and 0.31 M of that arrived through calls that passed no
`limit` at all. What is settled is only that rust-analyzer is the wrong
instrument for it — 26× the tokens on the common query. A `just` recipe that
addresses a source file by symbol rather than by line range is the same fix
`decision` was, and is not refused here. It is §57.7.

### 57.7 `just src`, and what validated it

`just src Decision` prints that enum with its doc comment and attributes, from
wherever in the workspace it is defined, and `just src new crates/rcad-geom`
narrows a name that is defined 43 times. **One definition prints the item; more
than one prints the places**, because printing every `fn new` in the workspace
is the cost the recipe exists to avoid.

The extent is read off rustfmt's layout rather than parsed: back to the blank
line above the definition, forward to the first `}` at the definition's own
indentation. That is a real assumption and it is why `just fmt` matters here,
so **it fails and says so when that brace is not there**, rather than printing
to the end of the file. An item that runs on for 7 000 lines is the failure the
recipe is against; producing one silently would be worse than not having it.

Across the 32 top-level functions of `arrange.rs` — 330 509 characters, the
largest file in the tree — every extraction ends on a brace at column 0, and the
mean extraction is 1 961 characters against the 6 541 of the largest. Across 149
items in four more large files, none was cut wrong; the single item the check
flagged was the check's own bug, since a tuple struct has no braces to balance.

The selftest earned its place immediately. With one file to search, `grep -n`
omits the filename, so `just src shared src/b.rs` — the narrowing case, the
whole point of the second argument — parsed the line number as the path and died
on a file called `1`. It is `-nH` now. A fixture repo is what caught it, because
the unfiltered searches that ran first all had more than one file and all
passed.

### 57.8 Two sections with one number, now caught

§57.4 said a split would not have fixed the number collision. It did not say
anything was catching it, and nothing was: `check-decisions` asked only whether
a heading had the right *shape*, so two `## 56.` headings passed it cleanly, and
`decision` stopped at the first of them. The second section was addressed by
nothing at all, silently. That is the same failure as a search that matches
nothing — an empty answer that reads like a clean one — and it is the third time
this file has recorded that shape.

It is not a typo's failure, which is why it is worth a check rather than care.
Sections are appended at the tail by whoever finishes first, ten to thirty times
a day, from as many as four concurrent sessions; two of them reaching for the
same next number is the ordinary case. It cost one manual renumber to find, at
merge time, by reading. `check-decisions` now names both offending lines and
fails.

The fixtures are duplicates rather than the real file, because the real file has
no duplicate today and pinning it there would prove nothing. Before the check,
the heading-shape grep found nothing wrong with a two-line file containing `## 1.`
twice; that is what the check-in demonstration ran.

## 58. The floor a mesh publishes is one the walk will take, recorded 2026-09-06

### 58.1 The unit, and why its record is late

Ten commits, `c9ff754..8358620`, in three lanes — floor, tolerant and import —
merged at `86b72c3` and closed with three documentation commits. It changed
`SolidView::room_a_mesh_has_to_work_in`, added two functions to `mesh.rs`, moved
what `Error::DeflectionBelowWhatAMeshCanReach` hands a caller, added five tests
across three files, and discharged `docs/consumers.md`'s announcement bullet for
the first time. **It left no section here at all.** This is that section, written
from the commits and from the tree rather than from anyone's report.

### 58.2 One number doing two jobs, and only one of them was its job

`room_a_mesh_has_to_work_in` is asked two different questions and had one answer
for both.

- **Let a caller's own deflection through, or refuse it.** The floor that belongs
  here is `how_far_a_mesh_point_of_this_face_rounds`: how close to the surface a
  mesh point can be **placed**, once the evaluator has rounded against how far
  the surface reaches and the placement has rounded again against how far the
  face reaches where the solid sits.
- **Pick a deflection for a tolerant caller who asked for finer than the
  arithmetic has.** Here there is nobody left to hand a refusal to. Whatever
  comes out of that line goes to `rcad_geom::walk` with no-one else looking at
  it.

The placing floor says nothing about **how many points** the walk will put along
one crossing, and the walk will not put more than
`MOST_POINTS_ALONG_ONE_CROSSING` of them. So the fallback handed the walk twice a
number the walk refuses, and a caller got
`rcad_geom::Error::TooManyPointsAlongOneCrossing { most: 1048576 }` for a
deflection this crate had just worked out itself. A round bar of radius one at
the origin, `Deflection::of(1e-300)`, `Policy::tolerant(100.0)`: four public
calls, no fuse, no import, no placement, nothing leaning.

`whether_the_floor_predicts_the_step_cap.rs`'s header carries how far short it
was: `4.8706` times from the step cap on its own, then divided by the three
sixteenths of the deflection the walk is actually handed, which is `25.98`, and
`walk`'s own deviation puts the crossover a little past twenty-six. The measured
bracket either side of it is between sixteen and thirty-two.

### 58.3 The fix: a second floor, and which one answers whom

`the_finest_deflection_the_walk_will_take` is the placing floor with one term
added — `how_far_a_step_at_the_cap_stands_off_its_chord`, what the arc of one
step stands off its own chord when a whole turn is walked in as many steps as the
walk allows. The added term goes in exactly where the evaluator's roundoff goes
in, so it pays the same two cuts on the way down: the movement into place comes
off the deflection before the walk is called, and the walk is handed
`WHAT_A_BOUNDARY_SIDE_IS_REFINED_TO` of what is left.

**Which floor is read depends on who chose the number, and that is the whole
design.** A caller who names a deflection is let through against the *placing*
floor and gets whatever the walk or the triangulator then says about the number
that caller chose. A deflection this crate picks is measured against the *walk*
floor, so the policy is asked about the number it will actually get. Asking a
policy about the first and then handing back the second is telling a caller its
budget was kept and then straying seventy-nine times further than it allowed.

`ROOM_ABOVE_THE_FLOOR` stays at `2.0` and its reason changed. It is no longer a
multiple of the placing floor, and no multiple of the placing floor would have
served: at the floor the walk asks `acos` for an angle three millionths of a
radian wide, where the subtraction in `1 − room/reach` has few digits left, and a
step count one over the cap is a refusal.

### 58.4 What `closest` carries now, and the separation, measured here

`DeflectionBelowWhatAMeshCanReach`'s `closest` used to be the placing floor and
is now the walk floor. That is a change to a published number and
`docs/consumers.md` records the announcement of it.

Re-measured for this section rather than copied, through a probe outside the tree
that calls only the public API: `Model::add_round_bar` / `Model::add_ball`, then
`SolidView::mesh` under `Policy::certified()`. The walk floor is read straight
out of the refusal's own `closest`. The placing floor is **hunted for** — bisect
for the deflection at which `DeflectionBelowWhatAMeshCanReach` stops being the
answer — which is the same hunt
`the_floor_under_a_deflection_stays_put_while_the_crossing_it_stands_for_runs_away`
makes, and neither number is worked out from the arithmetic that produces it.

| solid, asked `1e-300` | placing floor, hunted | walk floor, from `closest` | apart by |
|---|---|---|---|
| round bar, radius 1, height 2, at the origin | `9.214851104388813e-13` | `7.273230840146953e-11` | `78.92944506377196` |
| ball, radius 1, at the origin | `6.143234069592546e-13` | `4.848820560097969e-11` | `78.92944506377192` |

The ball's row is as measured for this section and is **superseded**: §58.11
halves both of its floors to `3.0716170347962663e-13` and
`2.4244102800489844e-11`. The bar's row and both ratios stand.

**The seventy-nine is a fact about the added term and not about either shape.**
Two solids that share no face agree on it to fifteen digits, because at the
origin `how_far_moving_this_face_rounds` is zero and the ratio collapses to
`(POINT_ALONG_A_CROSSING_ROUNDOFF + the step's stand-off) /
POINT_ALONG_A_CROSSING_ROUNDOFF`. It is not a factor to carry about: away from
the origin the movement term dominates both floors and they converge.

Two honesties about that table. The hunted column **converges from above** — a
hundred geometric halvings from `1e-300` stop at the first deflection not ruled
out, so it can sit a few `ulp` high, and the ball's reading is thirteen `ulp`
above the `6.143234069592533e-13` `mesh.rs` publishes while agreeing with it to
thirteen digits. And **the same hunt does not work far from the origin**: there
the first deflection above the placing floor is one the walk accepts, so the
probe meshes for real and does not finish — the wall
`whether_the_floor_predicts_the_step_cap.rs` names in *why there is no test here
that meshes at the new floor*. What this section did measure out there is the
walk floor alone, `3.9968513728593615e-6` for a unit ball at `x = 1e9`, which is
the figure `docs/consumers.md` announced. That one is **superseded by §58.11**
too, at `3.996827132753364e-6` — and it moved in the fifth figure where the pair
at the origin halved, because out there the placing term is eighty thousand times
the added one. It now has a test,
`a_unit_ball_a_thousand_million_units_out_is_cut_to_what_the_docs_announce`,
which it did not when this section was written.

### 58.5 Every bound this unit publishes, against the test that carries it

§15.6 says a published bound needs a test. Row by row, checked in the tree at
`99d6458`, where the three `rcad-topo` binaries this unit touches run 31 tests
and the `rcad-step` one runs 2, and all 33 pass.

| what is published, and where | carried by | holds? |
|---|---|---|
| `closest` names a deflection the walk will take (`error.rs`, `mesh.rs`) | `a_tolerant_caller_is_refused_by_the_floor_and_not_by_the_walk` | **in part** — see below |
| the mesher settles a fallback against its own floor instead of handing the walk a deflection it refuses | the same test, by the refusal's *name* | **yes** |
| a bar a billion units out still gets its old fallback, 5134 points and `5.99402529715387e-6` of deviation | `the_fallback_a_bar_a_billion_units_out_already_had_says_the_same_thing`, asserting both exactly | **yes** |
| a tolerant caller is refused as if its solid were broken where `room_left_over` gives up, over twelve cells | `a_tolerant_caller_is_refused_as_if_its_solid_were_broken_and_a_certified_one_is_not` | **yes** |
| those bars are not the thing that is wrong: built certified, empty provenance log, `validate` passes certified | `every_bar_in_the_table_is_built_and_checked_with_no_tolerance_asked_for` | **yes** |
| the mesher's floor stays put over four leans while the crossing's rounding runs away from it | `the_floor_under_a_deflection_stays_put_while_the_crossing_it_stands_for_runs_away` | **yes, as a shape** — no value asserted |
| styling is never a key in `shapes_this_reader_did_not_take`, and a styling-only file gets an `Err` rather than an empty map | `styling_is_never_among_the_shapes_walked_past`, over the real corpus | **yes** |
| `9.2148511043888e-13` and `7.273230840146953e-11`, the two floors of a bar of radius one at the origin (`mesh.rs`) | `a_round_bar_at_the_origin_places_a_point_a_thousand_times_closer_than_it_can_be_cut` | **yes**, since this section was written |
| `6.143234069592533e-13`, `4.848820560097969e-11` and *78.93 times apart* for a ball at the origin (`error.rs`) | `a_unit_ball_at_the_origin_places_a_point_a_thousand_times_closer_than_it_can_be_cut`, and the ratio on both shapes at once | **yes**, and the two floors are **superseded** by §58.11 — `3.0716170347962663e-13` and `2.4244102800489844e-11`. The ratio stands |
| `741 455` steps at twice the floor against `1 048 576` at it (`ROOM_ABOVE_THE_FLOOR`) | `what_twice_the_room_buys_a_walk_at_its_step_cap.rs`, which also pins the one-step margin and the design room the count belongs to | **yes**, since this section was written |
| the leaning-cap figures: a conic reach of `9.999999999999999e8` at `lean = 1e9`, a crossing rounding of `5.6843418889229724e-5`, a floor of `9.697641120195938e-11` (`mesh.rs`) | nothing, and nothing is owed — `f9d54e0` deleted the doc block that held all three | **withdrawn** |

**The first row is the one worth reading twice.** The test asserts
`closest > 1 − cos(π / MOST_POINTS_ALONG_ONE_CROSSING)` on a bar of radius one at
the origin, which is a **necessary** condition: below that the walk certainly
refuses. It is not the promise the unit is named for, which is that the
deflection the mesher then picks — `closest` through `ROOM_ABOVE_THE_FLOOR` and
two more cuts — is one the walk **accepts**. The tree says why not, and the
reason is honest: at twice the floor a bar's two cap circles come to about one
and a half million boundary points and the triangulator was still running after
two minutes. So the promise is checked from the refusal side and not from the
mesh side, and that is a gap this section names rather than one it hides.

**Three rows say *no test*, and they are one species**: a floor's value written
into a doc comment because somebody measured it once. §56.5 made exactly this
repair for the floor at a distance, and the same repair is available here — a
test that hunts for both floors of one shape at the origin and asserts the pair,
which is cheap because both refusals are immediate. **This section does not make
it**: this lane owns `docs/` only. It is recorded as owed.

**The fourth row is not owed, because the bound it asks for a test on no longer
exists.** It was written as a fourth *no test* and it is a **withdrawn** bound.
`f9d54e0` rewrote `the_finest_deflection_the_walk_will_take`'s doc block and
deleted all three numbers with it — the conic reach, the crossing rounding and
the floor — and that commit sits inside the reach under-charge unit, merged as
`74c14c7` immediately before this section was written. So the census read a tree
that had already moved under it and asked for a test on a number nothing
publishes any more. Deleting the row would hide that; a row that says *withdrawn*
and names the commit does not.

What the block says now is a different claim about a different tree. The wall's
reach is no longer `2` at every lean: `mesh.rs` records `2000001.5` at
`lean = 1e6` and `4000000001.5` at `lean = 2e9`, which is `2 · lean + 1.5`, the
way the ellipse itself climbs. Those two are a *shape* under test rather than two
asserted values — `what_a_leaning_cut_costs_the_floor_under_a_mesh.rs` divides
the floor by that oracle at four leans and asserts the four shares agree — and
the floors that come out of it are asserted to the last digit by
`what_floor_a_bar_with_a_leaning_cap_is_given.rs`.

### 58.6 The new floor is too low on a leaning cut, and this unit did not close it

`walk` charges its room against `Conic::how_far_it_reaches`, the crossing's own
longer semi-axis. Both floors charge `how_far_the_points_of_reach`, the face's
corners plus its surface's radius. **They are not the same number, and the second
is not always the bigger.** A bar of radius one cut by a leaning plane has its
ellipse walked as an edge of the *wall*, whose reach is `2` at every lean and
knows nothing about the plane; the conic's own reach grows with the lean without
bound.

So the fix's promise does not hold on that family, and `mesh.rs` says so in the
same breath as making it. It holds where a crossing is a circle no wider than the
surface it is cut on — every cap circle of a bar, every circle a plane cuts in a
ball — which is what the defect was about. On a leaning cut the change moved
**which refusal arrives** and did not earn an answer:
`TooManyPointsAlongOneCrossing` before, `AWireDoesNotFanIntoALoopToMesh` with
`TooFewCorners { count: 1 }` after, and neither is a mesh.

By §16.10 this is a **gap and not a limit**, and the family of fixes is named
rather than waved at: charge the crossings instead of the corners, and every
conic on the face has to be worked out before there is a deflection to walk one
with — the walk's own job, done twice. Bound the ellipse from the pair of
surfaces that cut it, and the floor stops being a question about one surface,
which is the thing that makes it cheap. Or keep the stand-in away from the
numbers it is wrong about, which is what is claimed today and is a claim about
**who chose the deflection**, not about a face's reach covering its crossings'.
The third is free and the tree takes it. Extending this floor to a caller-named
deflection would turn a floor that does not bind into a wrong answer.

**Everything above this line is the tree as it was, and the gap has since been
closed by the second of those three and not the third.** The reach under-charge
unit, merged as `74c14c7`, made `how_far_the_points_of_reach` bound a pipe's or a
cone's face along its own axis from the pair of surfaces either side of each of
its edges. `f9d54e0` inside it rewrote the doc block this section is reading, so
"whose reach is `2` at every lean" is no longer true of anything: the wall now
reaches `2 · lean + 1.5`. What survives is the narrow claim — a face's reach
still does not cover its crossings' where nothing along an edge bounds where that
edge runs, a cone met by a pipe on its own axis being such an edge. Only the
`Cylinder` and `Cone` arms moved: a ball and a ring are bounded surfaces, so
`Sphere` and `Torus` are still charged from their corners.

### 58.7 The step cap is a gap; the rounding under it is a limit

`DeflectionBelowWhatAMeshCanReach` now has two reasons behind one name and
`error.rs` keeps them apart. The rounding half is a **limit**: no `f64` point
sits closer to the surface, and §18's scaling reaches it exactly. The step-cap
half is a **gap**: the answer exists, `f64` reaches it, and a bigger cap hands it
back. It is deferred because a mesh at the cap is already a million points along
one circle and nobody has asked for two — §13, and the deferral is of a limit's
*neighbour*, so it is written down as owed rather than as impossible.

### 58.8 What a tolerant caller is told where the walk runs out of room

The tolerant lane measured a second thing and fixed none of it, which is the
right order. Where `rcad_geom`'s `room_left_over` runs out, a certified caller is
refused with `CannotPlaceAPointThatCloseToACrossing` carrying both numbers — how
much of the deflection was left to walk the crossing in, and how much the
crossing rounds by — and a tolerant caller is waved through with `Ok(None)`. The
walk then hands back a crossing with no points between its ends, a closed edge's
single corner becomes the whole of its wire, and the mesher answers
`AWireDoesNotFanIntoALoopToMesh { TooFewCorners { count: 1 } }`, which is the
name for a malformed solid.

**Neither caller gets a mesh and the tolerant one is told something untrue about
why.** Twelve cells, twelve of each, and the solids are built certified with an
empty provenance log and pass `validate` certified. `docs/consumers.md` records
a consumer that keeps an unrecognised refusal's debug text verbatim in its bug
reports, so this wording travels: what that consumer files for this is a corner
count and a face key, and not one of the two numbers that say what happened.

That is the third way to reach the four *malformed shape* refusals, and `mesh.rs`
now names all three: a solid that arrived from a file, a fuse that was wrong
about a block corner on a ball's pole, and this — a tolerant policy on a solid
nothing is wrong with.

### 58.9 The import lane, and where it is recorded

The third lane's finding — `Import`'s census reading as complete when styling is
read past uncounted — is §56.6, written by a different session that found the
same defect independently and dropped its own fix on finding this lane's. It is
not restated here. What belongs here is only that the lane is part of this unit
and that its test is in the table in §58.5.

### 58.10 What this does not close

1. **The leaning cut**, §58.6. A gap when this was written, with its family of
   fixes named and none of them taken. The reach under-charge unit, `74c14c7`,
   has since taken the second of them; what is left open is the fallback the
   closing paragraph of §58.6 names.
2. **The tolerant wave-through**, §58.8. Measured over twelve cells and not
   fixed. Any fix closes the window those twelve cells live in, and the file says
   so, so a red there would be the fix and not a regression.
3. **Three published numbers with no test**, §58.5. Owed, and cheap. A fourth row
   was counted here and is withdrawn rather than owed.
4. **The promise checked only from the refusal side**, §58.5. Whether the
   fallback should be held to a mesh that *finishes* as well as to one the walk
   accepts is a separate question, and no section has answered it.
5. **A caller-named deflection is still held to the placing floor and no other**,
   deliberately. Holding it to the step cap as well would make
   `TooManyPointsAlongOneCrossing` unreachable through `mesh`, which is a claim
   about the public API and wants its own demonstration.

## 59. A question the status line could not name, recorded 2026-09-06

The open questions of a session live in a file in that session's own scratchpad.
No section had recorded it before this one. It could be counted and it could not
be read: the status line said which labels were open, and getting the text of one
meant `!cat` on the whole file. This records the address that closed that, a
parser bug the work turned up, one recipe deliberately not built, and a number
this section corrects.

### 59.1 The address the file did not have

The file is `<tmp>/claude-<uid>/<slug>/<session>/scratchpad/open-questions.md`.
Every part of that is derivable except the session id, which only the harness
knows — so nothing a person can type names the file. The status line already had
the id, in its own input, and was throwing it away.

Six characters of it now print beside the labels, the width `just lanes` prints a
lane's ref in, and `just question <hash> <label>` takes that as the address.
`just question` alone lists the sessions that have open questions; with a hash
and no label it lists that session's labels and headings.

What this replaces is `!cat`, and the cost of `!cat` is not the reading. Shell
mode puts the output into the conversation, where it is charged again on every
later turn; `statusline.sh`'s own header records 21 command outputs and 5 710
characters put there that way on 2026-09-05. The file being read that way on
2026-09-06 held sixteen open questions, to get the text of one.

### 59.2 Fourteen of sixteen

An entry may carry two labels when one answer settles both, `**Q7 / Q11**`. The
parser matched the label once, so the second was neither counted nor shown.

Measured on the file as it stood at 10:18 on 2026-09-06: fourteen open checkbox
lines, two of them paired, so **sixteen open questions and fourteen labels on the
line**. The two that were invisible, Q11 and Q27, had been open all day. Run on
that file, the old parser prints fourteen labels and the new one sixteen.

**This corrects a published number.** `0828cb9`, the doc comment it added to
`statusline.sh`, and the paragraph it added to CLAUDE.md all say "thirteen of
fifteen". That is a miscount of the same file — the open lines were fourteen, not
thirteen — and it went in without being re-derived. The two files are corrected
in the commit that adds this section. The commit message cannot be, so this is
the record that it is wrong.

The failure is the shape §57.8 had recorded from another direction that same day:
a short answer that reads like a complete one. A status line whose whole job is
"what is waiting on you" is the last place that can under-report it, so the
labels are walked to the end of the run rather than matched once.

### 59.3 What is not built: a recipe that writes a question

A recipe that *asks* a question was proposed and declined. §13 is not what
declines it — the consumer exists, it is every session — so the argument belongs
here rather than in a deferral.

A body is paragraphs of prose carrying backticks, `§` refs and `**`. Passing one
through a shell argument means quoting all of that correctly, and it is never
cheaper than `Edit`: the text is written once either way, and whatever the recipe
prints is charged on top. The cost argument runs against the recipe, not for it.

The stronger reason is what the two operations are. Adding a question is an
append, which cannot silently match the wrong thing. Marking one answered is a
substitution, `- [ ]` to `- [x]`, and that is the shape §50.8 keeps out of the
shell: a pattern that does not match fails quietly, where `Edit` errors. A recipe
that did the append and not the substitution would be half a tool, and one that
did both would put the quiet half in the shell.

The model also has no addressing problem to solve — its own scratchpad path is in
its system prompt. The hash is for the person.

`just question <hash>` with no label took the place of a write-side check. It
reads labels through the same walk the status line uses, so an entry the line
would drop is missing there too.

### 59.4 The exemption the patching hook advertised but did not implement

Found while writing a fixture for the above, and fixed in the same run.

The hook refused `S=/tmp/…/scratchpad; cat > "$S/fixture.md"` and told the caller
"Writing under /tmp or a scratchpad is still fine". It judges the extracted
redirect fragment as text, so what it saw was `$S/fixture.md`, which matches
neither `^/tmp/` nor `scratchpad`. Failing closed is the right direction; saying
the opposite while doing it is not, and the caller it stops is a lane writing a
fixture to its own scratchpad — the case CLAUDE.md keeps Bash for.

Assignments made in the same command are now resolved before the path is judged.
Only the same command can matter: the Bash tool carries a working directory
between calls and no shell state, so a variable set in an earlier call is not set
here either. One that cannot be resolved stays unresolved, and unresolved is
still judged a tree file.

The guard is not loosened, and that is the half worth testing: a variable holding
`crates/rcad-geom/src` is still refused, and so is one this command never set.
Five cases, two of which the old hook gets wrong.

The hook then refused the command that would have added those five cases, because
it carried `> "$W/lib.rs"` as literal text. Its own header already describes
that: the cases live in JSON rather than in the runner for exactly this reason,
and it had blocked two earlier drafts of its own test.

### 59.5 What is still uncaught

`check-decisions` now fails on two sections sharing a number (§57.8, `cc969ad`),
so the collision this section's own numbering came close to repeating cannot
happen silently any more — §58 was taken between the number being chosen and the
section being written.

**It catches the collision at merge, which is later than it is made.** The check
reads one file, so it cannot see a number taken on a branch that has not landed.
On 2026-09-06 this section and "Nobody works in the hub" were both written as
§59, on two unmerged branches, and the duplicate was found by the other session
saying so — not by the check, which would have fired only when the second of them
merged. Four instances in one day, for a shape unnoticed across the fifty-seven
sections before it: one near-miss on 56, §58 taken mid-write, this collision, and
the renumber that settled it. Nothing watches the branches, and nothing is
proposed here that should: the check fires before anything is published, which is
the point at which being wrong costs something.

A heading deleted with its body left behind still can. The orphaned lines join
the section above, `decisions-toc` counts them there, and nothing says so. No
check is built for it, and no claim is made here that none is needed: it has not
cost anything yet, which is the only reason.

## 60. Nobody works in the hub, recorded 2026-09-06

§59 belongs to `rcad-c4`, which had claimed it in a worktree rather than in this
file. That is the same collision §55's preamble opens with and §57.8 built a
check for, and it happened again while this section was being written — so this
one moved rather than argue about it. The two sessions agreed by message, which
is a record that dies with them; the number in the heading is the one that does
not.

### 60.1 The tree the record cannot describe

§55 settled that a worktree's git lock is this repository's statement of who owns
it, and §55.4 gave the reason: it is the only candidate that survives the session
that wrote it. The alarm here was raised by a session trying to use it for
exactly that — announcing a ten-minute build before starting it — and finding
that it could not.

`git worktree lock` refuses the main working tree. There is no flag. So the one
tree that the record structurally cannot describe is the tree every session lands
in by default, and `just lanes` was printing `free` beside it whoever was
building in it. That is not a gap in the tooling; it is `lanes` reporting the
only thing git will tell it, which happens to be indistinguishable from an
answer.

The fix chosen is not a second record beside the lock. It is to delete the case:
**nobody works in the hub.** A tree nobody works in needs no owner, and `free`
becomes true about it rather than a guess.

### 60.2 The demonstration

Three refusals, all measured on 2026-09-06 in a repository built for the purpose.
The first is why the hub cannot be owned; the second and third are why `main`
cannot stay in it.

| what was tried | what git said |
|---|---|
| `git worktree lock --reason "test" .`, and by absolute path | `fatal: The main working tree cannot be locked or unlocked` |
| `git fetch . lane:main` from a lane, `main` checked out in the hub | `fatal: refusing to fetch into branch 'refs/heads/main' checked out at .../main` |
| `git push . lane:main`, same shape | `! [remote rejected] lane -> main (branch is currently checked out)` |

### 60.3 Why `main` leaving the hub is the load-bearing half

"Sessions use worktrees" on its own does not survive contact with a merge. Rows
two and three above say a branch checked out in the hub cannot be moved from
anywhere else, so every merge has to be performed *in* the hub — which is the one
moment when two sessions most need to know who is there, in the one tree that
cannot say. A rule that holds until the interesting moment and then breaks is
worse than none, because it is believed.

Parked on a detached HEAD the hub holds no branch, `main` is checkable out in a
worktree like any lane, and the merge tree is locked and named like any other.
This was already the live state when the section was written — `main` was checked
out and locked in `rcad-worktrees/wave-1`, held by a peer session mid-merge, and
the hub was detached. Somebody had reached the same design and not written it
down, which is the failure mode §55 was itself about.

### 60.4 What changed

| # | change | what proves it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `just check-hub` — fails when the hub has a branch checked out or uncommitted work in it; in `default` | `just check-hub-selftest`, in `default`; walks one fixture hub through lone-checkout, on-a-branch, dirty and parked, and asserts the middle two fail |
| 2 | `just lanes` labels the first tree `hub`, leaves it out of the lane count, and warns when it is not parked | `check-lanes-selftest`, extended; its fixture hub sits on a branch, so the warning is exercised |
| 3 | `.claude/hooks/session-start-hub.sh` tells a session that started in the hub to call `EnterWorktree` | `.claude/hooks/check-session-start-hub.sh`, in `check-hooks`; five cases, four of which assert *silence* |
| 4 | `just clean-targets` asks git for the worktrees instead of guessing a path, and so reaches the sibling trees and the hub's own 14 GB | `check-clean-targets-selftest`, in `default`; asserts the hub's `target/` goes and that a locked tree's survives |
| 5 | CLAUDE.md gains "Nobody works in the hub"; `delegating` gains never-merge-in-the-hub and a reclaim-and-re-park close | prose |

### 60.5 A silent sweep that had been silent for a month

Item 4 was meant to be a widening and turned out to be a bug fix. `clean-targets`
built the string `$(dirname $(git rev-parse --show-toplevel))/rcad-worktrees`,
which is the right answer only when it is run from the hub. Run from a lane it
resolved to `rcad-worktrees/rcad-worktrees`, found nothing, and printed *"there is
nothing here to clean"* — an empty answer wearing the clothes of a clean one, the
same shape as §57.8's and §55's. The rule in this section makes every run a run
from a lane, so it would have been every run from here on.

The disk was at 92% when this was found.

### 60.6 The exemption, and why it is structural

`check-hub` passes when the repository has exactly one worktree, because then
there is no hub and no lane, only a checkout, and no second session to collide
with. That is a fresh clone, and it is the shape a CI checkout has. CI runs
`check`, `lint`, `test` and `deny` rather than `default`, so the check does not
fire there today and the exemption is not load-bearing for the build — it is
what would keep it green if `default` ever moved into CI.

It is deliberately not an environment variable: an exemption that has to be set
is an exemption that gets set, whereas this one lapses by itself the moment a
second tree exists, which is the moment ownership starts being a question.

### 60.7 What this does not close

**Nothing stops a session working in the hub.** The session-start hook is a
notice and `check-hub` is a check; both can be ignored until the next `just
default`. The mechanical version is a `PreToolUse` hook that refuses `Edit` and
`Write` there — `no-in-place-rust-patching.sh` is the precedent — and it is
deliberately not built: §13 wants the consumer named first, and it would also
refuse Mattias's own `!` commands in the directory he starts in, which is a cost
worth paying only once the cheap version is shown to leak.

**Nothing re-parks the hub either.** After a merge the hub sits on whatever
commit it was detached at, and it is a person or the closing gate that moves it
forward. That is the safe direction to fail — a stale hub is harmless where a hub
holding `main` is not — but §55.6's "an abandoned lock is rubbish only a person
clears" now has a sibling.

### 60.8 Untracked counts, and `fuzz/corpus/` is not ignored

`rcad-c4` asked the two questions this section had answered only by implication,
and both deserve the record rather than the implication.

**Untracked-and-unignored is uncommitted work.** A check that looked only at
tracked modifications would have passed the hub all evening while it held the
single most valuable thing at risk: 1542 corpus entries a fuse campaign had
earned and left there. When the campaign moved to a worktree it started from the
tracked 1088, so those 1542 existed in exactly one place, and that place was the
tree nobody owns. They are now committed — replaying takes the corpus from
`cov: 13342 ft: 54505` to `cov: 14123 ft: 65660`, so they were coverage and not
noise. A rule that ignored untracked files would have been silent about precisely
the harm it exists to prevent.

**`fuzz/corpus/` stays tracked.** The suggestion was to ignore it so that a fuzz
run stops dirtying whatever tree it is in. That is backwards: 3999 corpus entries
are committed on purpose, `fuzz/.gitignore` names `artifacts/`, `coverage/` and
`target/` and pointedly not `corpus/`, and a seed corpus that is not shipped is a
fuzzer that starts from nothing on every machine. The dirt a campaign leaves is
not the problem; leaving it in the hub is. The remedy is the rule, not an
exemption from it — and the exemption would have thrown away tonight's 1542.

**What no check here can see.** The collision that sent this section from §59 to
§60 was caught by one session telling another, not by `check-decisions`, which
reads one file and so fires when the second branch *merges* rather than when the
number is taken. §59.5 records that from the other side. It is the same fact as
this section's: two sessions cannot see each other's work in progress, and the
answer is a record that outlives the session — a lock, a heading, a commit — not
a smarter check. Firing at publication is the right time; nothing above claims
otherwise.

### 60.9 A stale hub is not leftovers, and the message has to know which

§60.7 called an un-re-parked hub harmless. It is harmless to the *repository* and
it was not harmless to this check, which `rcad-c4` spotted before it bit anyone:
a hub parked at an older commit shows every path that has landed since as
untracked, indistinguishable by `status` from work somebody abandoned there. The
symptom is one thing and the two causes want opposite fixes, so the message that
says "commit this from a worktree of your own" sends a reader to duplicate a
merge that has already happened.

They are told apart by asking git rather than by guessing: if nothing is modified
and **every** untracked path is already in `ls-tree main`, the hub is behind, not
dirty. `check-hub` then names the command that fixes it and says that nothing
moves the hub's HEAD on its own. `check-hub-selftest` builds that state — a file
committed on `main` from a lane, present on disk in a hub whose HEAD predates it
— and asserts both that the stale message appears and that the leftovers message
does not.

**The first remedy this section printed did not work.** It was
`git -C <hub> checkout --detach main`, on the reasoning that files whose content
already matches the target commit cannot be at risk. Git does not reason that
way. It refuses on the paths alone:

    error: The following untracked working tree files would be overwritten by checkout:
            fuzz/corpus/aaa
    Please move or remove them before you switch branches.

Measured both ways in a throwaway repository: byte-identical content aborts, and
differing content aborts with the same message, so the two are indistinguishable
from the output. `git clean -fd` first, then the checkout, exits 0, restores
every file byte-identical, and leaves `git status` empty. The published line is
therefore `git -C <hub> clean -fd && git -C <hub> checkout --detach main`, and
`clean` without `-x` leaves ignored files alone, so a campaign's crash artifacts
survive it.

So the files are deleted either way. "Re-parking makes them tracked rather than
deleted" was argued between the two sessions and never reached this file, which
is the only reason it is not a correction to a published paragraph. What survives
of it is the *timing*: deleting at re-park time is safe because by then the
content is on `main`, where deleting before the merge would have left
`lane-hub-rule` as the only copy.

**The selftest runs the line the check prints**, greps it back out of the output,
executes it, and asserts the hub lands on `main`, that `status` comes back empty,
that the removed file is restored, and that `check-hub` then passes. A remedy
nobody executes is a claim without a test, which is §15.6's rule pointed at a
string rather than at a bound. Restoring the old one-command version fails it
with *"the remedy the check prints does not run"*.

Found by `rcad-c4` running it rather than reading it — twice over, since §60.7's
"harmless" is what pointed them at the case to begin with. Both defects were in
prose that had been reviewed and neither was in code that had been tested, which
is the argument for the paragraph above.

### 60.10 The same name is not the same file

§60.9's test for "the hub is only behind" was **every untracked path is already
in `ls-tree main`**. That compares names. It stood in front of a `clean -fd` that
deletes those same paths, so a file in the hub whose name is on `main` but whose
bytes are not was told it was safe and then removed.

Demonstrated in a throwaway repository rather than argued. A hub parked one
commit back, holding `notes.txt`:

    hub blob:  3efd841a4fa917602af4c8547eb46d369b94a4d1
    main blob: 56985387e75729cd805934b2322e7d79ff9bd594

`check-hub` answered *"Every one of those is already committed on `main`, so
nothing here is lost work"* and printed its remedy. Running that remedy: the file
afterwards holds `main`'s version, and the hub's content is reachable from no ref
at all. It was never in a commit; there was nothing to recover it from.

**It could not have bitten on 2026-09-06, and that is luck rather than design.**
The 1542 were libfuzzer corpus entries, which are named by the hash of their
contents, so for them a matching name *did* imply matching bytes. `check-hub`
does not know that, and nothing restricts it to `fuzz/corpus/`. A hub parked
behind `main` with a half-written `docs/notes.md` in it, while a lane lands a
different `docs/notes.md`, is the same shape with a person's work in it.

The check now hashes each path and compares against `main:<path>`. It enumerates
with `ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z` rather than reading `status`,
which reports an untracked directory as a single entry and quotes awkward names.
The one thing `clean -fd` removes that this does not hash is an empty directory,
which holds nothing to lose.

**The old fixture could not fail.** It wrote `landed` with the same content on
both sides, so a name-only comparison and a content comparison agreed on it —
the test passed for a reason weaker than the one it was believed to prove. The
new case writes different bytes under the same name and asserts the "already
committed" sentence does *not* appear. Put the name-only comparison back and it
fails with *"content that is on no branch was called committed, and the remedy
deletes it"*.

**Two more things measured during the re-park, both about the same remedy.**

`checkout --detach main` does **not** restore a tracked file deleted in the
working tree when that file is identical in the old commit and the new one.
Checkout writes only what differs between the two, so the deletion survives it —
and checkout *prints* `D <path>` while doing nothing about it, which is the one
line a reader would scan for reassurance. A separate `git restore -- <path>` is
required. This bit a real file: a `crash-*` sweep had deleted
`fuzz/corpus/no_model_makes_the_writer_panic/crash-a54b24c9…`, a tracked seed
from `ce2dbf2` that is named like an artifact but is not one, and the re-park's
own assertion is what caught that the checkout had left it deleted.

`git clean -fd` will not remove a nested linked worktree — measured on **git
2.43.0**, with `.git` confirmed to be a file rather than a directory, `clean -nd`
listing it as no candidate at all. `git clean -ffd` removes it, taking
uncommitted work with it and leaving the registration `prunable`, which `just
lanes` then reports as `missing`. So the protection is a property of `clean`
stopped at one `-f`, not of `clean`; the published remedy must never gain a
second. The version is part of the claim because `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the
compiler and `mise.toml` pins the tooling, and nothing here pins git — §15.6 for
why a bound without its conditions is not a bound, and `dc650e7` for what
happens to a "the guard holds" sentence that travels without them.

**A worktree made from the hub lands inside the hub.** `git worktree add
rcad-worktrees/<name>` run with the hub as the working directory creates
`<hub>/rcad-worktrees/<name>`, not the sibling directory of the same name. An
empty `rcad-worktrees/` had been sitting in the hub since 2026-09-06 08:42 from
exactly that slip, and it went silently into the re-park's delete set — noticed
only because a dry run counted 1543 where 1542 had been verified. `rcad-c4` then
made the identical mistake while opening the lane for this section, which is the
evidence that it is easy rather than careless. Absolute paths in `worktree add`.

## 61. A wall of a box turned round, recorded 2026-09-07

`just fuzz-fuse` found ten crashes in 600 s. All ten are one bug, none of them
is in the fuse, and what they are is `Model::validate` accepting a solid whose
skin does not close. The fuse then walks it and trips `Model::check_touched_edge`
— an assert where a refusal belonged, §38.2's family — and in a **release**
build not even that: `check_touched_edge` returns early and `assemble`'s
post-write sweep is `debug_assertions`-gated, so two flat boxes with one wall
turned round fuse to `Ok` and commit a model that does not validate. That is
core principle 1 inverted, and it is what makes this a unit rather than a
hardening exercise.

Two ways in, both through `FaceUse`: `orient: Reversed` on a face of a box
(seven of the ten), and a `loc` that is not the identity (the other three).

### 61.1 The rule was written down twice and read back nowhere

`Assembly::write_into` (`fuse/assemble.rs:343`) and `rcad-step`'s
`describe_the_face` (`brep.rs:117`) keep the same table, and `brep.rs` calls it
"the same two-line table the fuse already keeps":

```text
(Some(flat), true)      => (Surface::Plane(flat.reversed()), Forward)
(Some(_) | None, false) => (piece.surface,                   Forward)
(None, true)            => (piece.surface,                   Reversed)
```

A plane welds "which surface" to "which way", so a plane facing the other way is
stored turned round and then used **forwards**; a sphere and a pipe have no
turned-round form, so those carry the turn on the face use. **No face sitting on
a plane is ever used reversed**, and until now nothing said so.

`Model::check_no_flat_face_is_used_reversed` is that sentence read back, in the
sweep and at the `Deserialize` door both. It reads the turn the *solid* ends up
using rather than the one written on the face, because nothing in the crate
writes a reversed `ShellUse` but `Deserialize` will read one and it turns every
face of that shell round.

### 61.2 Why nothing else could see it

Turning one wall of a box round changes no coedge in the model, so
`check_edge_is_walked_by_two_opposite_coedges` — which reads the turns as
stored — sees nothing. The wall's own winding is unchanged, because reversing a
face turns its normal *and* walks its wire the other way, and `check_flat_face`
reads the raw face at `Isometry::identity()` and never sees how a shell uses it
at all. What is left is the volume, and flipping one wall of a `10³` box leaves
the divergence sum at `333.3` — still positive, still no complaint.

It is reachable through the public API and not only through a file, which is
§16.11's kind: `SolidBuilder::add_shell` takes an `Orientation` per face and its
own door reads the stored turns too, so a box described face by face with any one
wall turned round built and validated.

### 61.3 The mesh answer was tried and is wrong

The obvious fix is to run `every_side_of_the_skin_is_used_both_ways` over a
wholly flat solid as well as a curved one, and the balance really does separate
the flipped box from the sound one — 4 sides not used both ways against 0, over
18 sides.

**It refuses sound solids.** `check_shells_and_solids` gives a polyhedron no mesh
because its own fan *is* its volume, and a fan cannot refuse; a mesh can.
`the_edge_across_a_sliver_is_as_long_as_the_sliver_is` comes back
`CannotMeshAFace { CoordinateOutOfRange { position: 2, why: TooSmall } }`, so a
sound fuse answer stops validating — a refusal about the sweep rather than about
the model, which is the thing `as_coarse_as_a_mesh_gets` exists to keep the
curved branch clear of. Meshing every flat solid at every test boundary is also
what §4.3 says not to spend.

### 61.4 And no count over the skin works either

The next candidate is that the two faces along an edge walk it opposite ways *as
their shell uses them*. It is wrong, and it is wrong for a reason §36.24 already
recorded: a curved face turned round is **the same surface with its wire stored
walked the other way**, so a bar's wall used reversed walks its open edges the
same way as the planes notching it and is perfectly sound. Measured, it refused
`every_answer_over_a_block_turned_against_a_bar_is_a_solid_that_validates` and
three STEP corpus tests. `a_washer`'s hole says the same thing about closed
edges, which is what the earlier attempt on this had found.

So a torn skin and a sound one are combinatorially identical, and only a plane —
which is welded to a direction — can be asked without arithmetic. That is why the
check is the table above and not a balance.

### 61.5 The placement half, and what it retires

A `FaceUse` carrying a placement tears the skin without moving a corner.
`FaceView` hands its own location down to its wires, so a displaced face reads
its surface *and* its corners at the same place and stays self-consistent —
every check that looks at one face passes, the volume is right. What stops being
true is that the two faces along an edge agree where that edge is. The mesh
cannot see it either, because the mesher names a corner by its vertex and both
faces name the same vertex: a wall moved 1000 units away and a wall nudged 0.25
both validated.

**Decision: `FaceUse::loc` must be the identity, refused at the door.** Every
site in the crate writes one, `place_solid` composes onto the *shell's*
placement and never the face's (§44.8), and a face is used by exactly one shell,
so there is no sharing for a per-use placement to serve — §42.7's argument about
shells, made about faces by `Invalid::UsedMoreThanOnce`. The alternative,
checking that the faces along each edge place it identically, is a pass over
pairs and a decision about how near is near enough, which is a tolerance this
kernel exists to avoid. Taking the field away was the third option and is not
needed: an identity that must stay an identity costs one comparison.

What it retires is `a_location_on_a_shell_and_one_on_a_face_compose`, which put a
shift on every face use and checked the two levels composed. They do, and
`SolidView::faces` still composes them; there is no longer any way to reach it.
The shell half of §3.2 is what a caller actually has, and
`a_face_reached_through_a_placed_solid_comes_back_already_moved` is where that
lives.

### 61.6 The door, and the tests that could no longer build what they tested

Both checks go in `check_shape_is_possible` as well as in the sweep. §44.5's rule
admits them — one pass over the face uses, an `Orientation` or an `Isometry`
against a constant, nothing about a pair — and it matters because `Model::fuse`
does not validate its arguments, so a model read off a wire and handed straight
to the fuse is exactly the shape the fuzzer found.

The cost is that two tests built their inside-out cube by turning all six face
*uses* round, which is no longer a model at all.
`a_solid_turned_inside_out_is_caught` and
`measuring_a_solid_read_back_inside_out_is_refused_rather_than_crashing` now
build it the way a file has to — every plane turned round, and every wire walked
the other way so that it still winds with the normal it is given. Written that
way no single face is wrong and neither is any single wire, so the volume is
still the only thing that can notice, which is what both were for.
`a_solid_described_with_every_face_turned_round_is_refused_by_the_sweep` still
comes back from the sweep and now names the rule that was broken rather than the
consequence.

### 61.7 What it is measured against

**The instrument that found it, run again at the same budget.** 614 s of
`two_solids_fused_by_a_stranger` at `-fork=4`, 3 439 084 executions,
`oom/timeout/crash: 0/0/0`, against ten crashes from 600 s of the same target
the day before.

All ten crash artifacts also replay with no crash, and **that on its own is weak
evidence** — an artifact the target now declines to decode never reaches the
fuse, and an invocation that ran nothing would look the same. What carries it is
the reduced forms beside them, which have a before. `face4_reversed.bin`,
`face4_moved.bin` and `face4_nudged.bin` used to decode and validate and now do
not decode; `55f28d44_first.bin`, which used to answer with a model that does not
validate, no longer decodes either. The sound controls in the same directory —
`built_only.bin` and the seven negative-zero variants — still decode, fuse and
validate, which is the half that makes the other half mean anything.

### 61.8 What this leaves

**`SolidBuilder::add_shell` could refuse a reversed flat face at the call rather
than at the sweep.** The draft's surface is known there, and the builder's own
division is that what one call can decide is decided there. It is one face and
not the whole solid, so by that division it belongs at the call.
`a_solid_described_with_every_face_turned_round_is_refused_by_the_sweep` is the
test that would move with it.

**A reversed `ShellUse` is still a thing a file can write.** Nothing in the crate
writes one and nothing reads one for anything but composition. It is caught here
only through what it composes onto a flat face; a solid of nothing but curved
faces with its shell used reversed is left to the volume.

## 62. A sweep that could only ever return one answer, recorded 2026-09-07

A fourth way a written-down finding stops being worth what it looked worth, and
it is not the three in `docs/consumers.md` — those are all *the world moved under
a true sentence*, and this one is *the sentence was never able to be true*. The
shape:

> **A sweep whose sample set could only ever return one of the two answers.** The
> run completes, the samples are real, every assertion passes — and the finding
> was settled before the first sample was drawn, because the sample set could not
> have produced the other one.

§16.11 is the nearest neighbour and is a different failure: there a check was
right about what it caught and every sentence citing it was reasoning about the
other half. Here the measurement is right, the sentences about it are right, and
the *sample set* is the thing that was never able to say the other thing.

The unifying statement across all four, which `docs/consumers.md` also carries
and which rscene asked be credited to this side:

> The artefact stayed internally consistent while the world it described moved,
> or was never fully sampled — and review checks consistency.

The first three arms are the *moved* half. This is the *never fully sampled*
half, and it is the one that says why a reading pass catches none of them.

### 62.1 The instance, and nothing in it was wrong

`crates/rcad-geom/tests/what_the_dynamic_range_check_is_a_margin_against.rs`
asks how small a wedge's feature can get against its coordinates before the apex
rounds onto the base and `orient3d` answers `Zero` about a model nobody built.
As first written it swept the coordinate at `1`, `2^10`, `2^20` and `2^40`.

Measured here at `b4e698f` by reading the bit patterns: all four have a mantissa
of exactly zero. That is the whole defect. A feature of exactly half an ulp puts
the apex exactly halfway between two doubles, round-half-to-even then decides,
and a zero mantissa is the even side of every such tie — so all four coordinates
round the same way, and a **cliff** was the only shape of answer the sample set
could return. It returned one, and it looked complete returning it.

**Nothing it asserted was false and the code under it was not buggy.** Worth
saying plainly, because it is what makes the arm hard to see: the run was green
for the right reason, on real samples, about real arithmetic. Its verdict — that
the spread the kernel publishes as supported sits far below where a written
feature dies — stands untouched, and one binade of head-room on half the
coordinates does not move it. The failure is that the run *looked complete*.

### 62.2 What the axis it held still actually does

Another lane sampled every representable placement across a whole binade and
found the law, in `rcad-topo`'s
`tests/how_far_out_a_ball_can_sit_and_still_mesh.rs`: refusal is **not monotone
in where a solid stands**. For a ball of radius `r` centred at `c` everything is
`r / ulp(c)`:

- above a half, the poles land in different ulp buckets and it meshes wherever
  it stands;
- below a half, both poles round back onto `c` and it refuses wherever it
  stands — and this does not depend on `c` at all;
- at exactly a half the poles sit on a tie, and round-half-to-even decides on
  the last bit of `c`'s mantissa. Even rounds inward and refuses; odd rounds
  outward and meshes.

`ulp` is constant across a binade, so the third case is not a knife edge: it
holds for a whole factor-of-two stretch, and the answer flips at every
representable placement in it. That lane's census — **32 meshed and 32 refused
over 64 consecutive placements** — is **their** measurement, not one re-taken
here. What was re-run here at `b4e698f` is the file itself: 13 tests, 13 passed.

A cliff cannot produce that. It cannot even produce the report that started it:
two placements, the lower refusing and the higher meshing, which is the one pair
a threshold of any height is forbidden to explain.

### 62.3 Why this is a category and not carelessness

**rcad-51's sentence, kept as they wrote it, because it is the section:**

> The `COORDINATES` doc comment reasoned explicitly about its sampling and still
> missed the axis, **because powers of two are simultaneously the natural thing
> to sweep and the one family with no mantissa to be odd**.

The obvious choice and the blind choice were the same choice. That is what earns
this a name of its own. A thoughtful comment was not the missing ingredient —
the thoughtful comment had been written, and read, and it argued about the
sampling and came out blind anyway, because the argument was about spanning the
range and the blindness was one bit below where it was looking.

It also rules out the two repairs that suggest themselves. *"Never sample only
powers of two"* is too narrow: powers of two are the right sample for a question
about magnitude, and the next instance of this will be some other convention
that happens to be constant in whatever the next answer turns on. *"Sample
more"* is useless and, here, wrong — the fix went from four coordinates to
eight and did not go one step finer in magnitude.

**A second instance, and it is rcad-51's own, committed within the hour of
writing the argument above.** Asking which files under `crates/rcad/tests`
mention `rcad_geom`, it grepped for `rcad_geom` and not for the hyphenated
`rcad-geom` that prose uses. The natural spelling and the blind spelling were
the same choice, one level down from the powers of two.

**Its own qualification, which goes in with it.** The load-bearing claim — which
files *import* `rcad_geom` — was never at risk, because a Rust import can only be
spelled with the underscore, so the narrow pattern found every import there was.
What the sample set could not reach was the claim actually written down, which
was about **mentions**. Re-measured here at `b4e698f`:
`grep -rn "rcad_geom\|rcad-geom" crates/rcad/tests crates/rcad/benches` gives six
hits across four files, `grep -rn "rcad_geom::" …` gives one, and there is no
`crates/rcad/examples`. So five of the six are prose, and a grep for the
underscore alone sees one of six while answering a question about all six.

That makes it the muddier illustration: it is two arms at once, a blind sample
set **and** a sentence that drifted off its evidence, and only the first of those
is this section. Where it is genuinely the stronger one is that its blind sample
set was **a spelling a person chose**. Nothing about binary floating point is
available to explain it away, which is rcad-51's point and their framing: the
fourth arm is about the **sampler, not the sampled**, and a sampler is as blind
in a grep pattern as in a `COORDINATES` array.

### 62.4 The rule, sharp enough to use before writing a sweep

**A sweep is blind exactly when its sample set has fewer degrees of freedom than
the answer does.** So, before running it:

1. Name every quantity the answer can turn on — not the ones being swept, all of
   them. Rounding puts more on that list than the shape does: exponent,
   mantissa, parity of the last bit, sign, which side of a tie.
2. For each, name **two samples in the set that differ on it and agree on
   everything else.** Not "the set covers a wide range" — two named members.
3. Anything with no such pair is a **constant of the run**, not a variable. The
   finding is then a statement about that constant, and it should be written
   down as one or the sample set should be widened until it is not.

Step 2 is the whole rule. It is the one that fails on this instance and it fails
in one line: for *parity of the last mantissa bit*, there is no such pair among
`1`, `2^10`, `2^20`, `2^40`, because all four are zero.

The trap the rule is aimed at: **the family reached for by convention is usually
the family with the fewest degrees of freedom.** Powers of two are the canonical
case — what anyone would pick to span a range, and constant in the one bit this
answer turned on — but tidy integers, unit radii, the origin and the identity
placement are the same trap. Convention is what makes a family easy to write
*and* what makes every member of it agree.

**What it costs**, and it is not nothing. Step 1 wants somebody who knows what
the arithmetic can turn on, which is the expensive ingredient and is not
purchasable by sampling harder. Step 2 costs a doubling of the sample set per
axis it finds — here 4 coordinates became 8 and the run stayed instant, but an
axis found in a family that already takes minutes is a real bill, and it is
sometimes right to name the constant instead of paying it. Naming it is the
cheap outcome and it is a legitimate one: *"this is a statement about even
mantissas"* is a true, useful, much smaller finding than the one that was
claimed.

### 62.5 The standing form: make the sweep prove it saw both answers

Steps 1-3 are done by a person once. What stops the sample set silently
narrowing again is an assertion, and the fixed file carries it:
`the_spread_a_written_feature_survives_to` counts how many coordinates kept the
feature at the tie and how many lost it, and asserts the two counts are
**equal** — with a message saying the sweep is not sampling both sides of the
tie and can only report one cliff. Measured here at `b4e698f` from the test's own
output: *"a written feature survives to a spread of `2^52` at worst and `2^53`
at best; at the tie 4 kept the feature and 4 swallowed it; 108 still there, 44
gone."*

That is a **positive control on the sample set**, and it is the same argument
§56.7 makes about an absence that could not have been a presence, one level
down: there the control proves the sweep could have failed, here it proves the
sweep could have answered the other way. §42.12's tenth criterion is the same
idea for a rate.

It is also §15.6's rule pointed at a sample set rather than at a bound. A
published bound wants a test; a published finding wants a test that the sample
set could have contradicted it.

### 62.6 The `testing` skill already had this, and what it does not reach

*"Vary what the family cannot vary, not just more of what it can"* is in the
skill already, under **"A second family for what the first cannot draw"**. Read
in full rather than skimmed to its examples, it goes further than those examples
suggest: its two worked cases are shapes — the notched star whose corners never
give two edges overlapping bounding boxes, and `a_simple_polygon` beside it —
but its closing clause is *"the knots in the spline families are not all small
whole numbers for the same reason"*, and a knot value is a number. **"Not all
small whole numbers" is already a warning against a degenerate numeric sample
set.** So the rule covers a family's parameters, numbers included, and asking it
to say "this is about numbers too" would be redundant with a clause it already
has. Saying so explicitly here, because a section about sample sets that only
sampled the two shape examples would be its own subject matter.

**What the rule does not reach is the coordinates a family is *placed at*.**
Those are not parameters of the family. Nothing in the family generates them,
shrinking never touches them, and a family drawn entirely correctly can be
evaluated at one placement for its whole life. They are the arithmetic context
the family runs in — and they are the axis both defects behind this section were
blind on.

So the sentence that is missing is: **a family's placement is part of its sample
